clips.text: This is how I sound reading your notes.
Prefix and suffix sums

Answer any range-sum question in O of 1 after one O of n pass, combine best-from-the-left with best-from-the-right around a split, and turn "count the subarrays with property X" into counting equal prefix values.

Store P of i is A of 0 plus … plus A of i minus 1 once; the sum of any block A from l to r is then P of r plus 1 minus P of l, so each query costs O of 1 after O of n work, and the same holds on a grid with inclusion–exclusion. The bigger payoff is that a condition on a subarray becomes a condition on a pair of prefix values: "this block sums to zero" means P of r plus 1 is P of l, so finding or counting such blocks is finding or counting equal values, in O of n log n with a sort or a map. Suffix arrays are the mirror image: precompute the best answer ending at each index (left to right) and starting at each index (right to left), then try every split point in O of 1 each.
clips.script: Store P of i is eh of 0 plus … plus eh of i minus 1 once; the sum of any block eh from l to r is then P of r plus 1 minus P of l, so each query costs O of 1 after O of n work, and the same holds on a grid with inclusion–exclusion. The bigger payoff is that a condition on a subarray becomes a condition on a pair of prefix values: "this block sums to zero" means P of r plus 1 is P of l, so finding or counting such blocks is finding or counting equal values, in O of n log n with a sort or a map. Suffix arrays are the mirror image: precompute the best answer ending at each index (left to right) and starting at each index (right to left), then try every split point in O of 1 each.

clips.text: Reach for it when
Many queries for the sum or count of something over a range l to r, with no updates in between.
Count (or find) subarrays whose sum is k, whose sum is their length, or whose two kinds of items balance out.
Remove one element, cut the array once or choose a pivot: the answer combines something about everything to the left with something about everything to the right.
A small grid (up to about 1000 times 1000) with many rectangle-sum queries.
Common bugs

Off-by-one between inclusive ranges and P: with P of size n plus 1, sum A from l to r is P of r plus 1 minus P of l. Forgetting P of 0 is 0 also forgets every subarray that starts at the first element.
clips.script: Off-by-one between inclusive ranges and P: with P of size n plus 1, sum eh from l to r is P of r plus 1 minus P of l. Forgetting P of 0 is 0 also forgets every subarray that starts at the first element.

clips.text: Overflow: 2 times 10 to the 5 values of 10 to the 9 already pass 2 to the 31, and counts of pairs reach n squared over 2, so keep prefix sums and answers in long long.
unordered map keyed on prefix sums can be broken by anti-hash tests on Codeforces; sort the prefix array, use map, or use a plain array shifted by an offset when the range of values is small.
How it hides in a statement
Count adjacent equal pairs, or positions with some property, inside l to r: that is, prefix count of a zero-one indicator array
Subarray whose sum is its length, or where two kinds of items balance: that is, subtract 1 from every element (or negate one kind), then look for two equal prefix sums
Delete one element / cut the array into parts / choose a pivot: that is, best-from-the-left and best-from-the-right arrays, then try every split in O of n
Best block to reverse, flip or swap: that is, write down the gain of each position, then maximise P of r minus min P of l over l at most r (maximum subarray sum)
P of i will hold the sum of the first i values of A. Start with P of 0 is 0, the empty prefix.
clips.script: P of i will hold the sum of the first i values of eh. Start with P of 0 is 0, the empty prefix.

clips.script: P of 1 is P of 0 plus eh of 0, which is 0 plus 3, so 3.

clips.text: A of 2 plus … plus A of 5 is P of 6 minus P of 2, which is 23 minus 4, so 19. Any range costs one subtraction: O of 1.

clips.text: Zero-sum blocks: b from l to r sums to 0 exactly when Q of l is Q of r plus 1. Walk the prefix sums Q, counting each value seen so far.
Q of 1 is Q of 0 plus b of 0, so 2, a value not seen before: no zero-sum block ends at 0.
Q of 2 is Q of 1 plus b of 1, so 1, a value not seen before: no zero-sum block ends at 1.
Q of 3 is Q of 2 plus b of 2, so 4, a value not seen before: no zero-sum block ends at 2.
Q of 4 is 2 was seen before, at Q of 1: b from 1 to 3 sums to 0. Blocks so far: 1.
Q of 5 is 0 was seen before, at Q of 0: b from 0 to 4 sums to 0. Blocks so far: 2.
Q of 6 is 4 was seen before, at Q of 3: b from 3 to 5 sums to 0. Blocks so far: 3.
3 zero-sum blocks, one per pair of equal prefix values, found in one pass with a hash map: O of n.
Difference arrays and sweeps

Apply many range updates in O of 1 each and read the result with one prefix pass, stack two levels when the updates come in ranges themselves, and sweep sorted events when coordinates are too large for an array.

A difference array stores d of i is A of i minus A of i minus 1. Adding v to A from l to r changes only two entries (d of l plus-equals v, d of r plus 1 minus-equals v), and one prefix-sum pass turns d back into A, so m range updates followed by reads cost O of n plus m instead of O of n times m. Stack it twice when the updates themselves come in ranges (a range of operations, or adding 1, 2, …, k to a segment). When coordinates reach 10 to the 9 or 10 to the 18, keep the same +v / minus v events but sort them and sweep: the value is constant between consecutive event coordinates, so you add up lengths instead of indexing an array.
clips.script: A difference array stores d of i is eh of i minus eh of i minus 1. Adding v to eh from l to r changes only two entries (d of l plus-equals v, d of r plus 1 minus-equals v), and one prefix-sum pass turns d back into eh, so m range updates followed by reads cost O of n plus m instead of O of n times m. Stack it twice when the updates themselves come in ranges (a range of operations, or adding 1, 2, …, k to a segment). When coordinates reach 10 to the 9 or 10 to the 18, keep the same +v / minus v events but sort them and sweep: the value is constant between consecutive event coordinates, so you add up lengths instead of indexing an array.

clips.text: Many "add v to every element from l to r" operations, and the values are only read after all of them.
For each point, how many intervals cover it, or how many points are covered by exactly k intervals.
You choose one value x from a large range, and each item contributes a cost that is constant on a few intervals of x.
Operations applied over a range of operation numbers, or operations that add an arithmetic progression to a segment.
The closing update d of r plus 1 lands one past the last index; size the array n plus 2 (or the largest coordinate plus 2).
Coordinates up to 10 to the 9 or 10 to the 18 do not fit in an array: switch to sorted (coordinate, ±v) events with r plus 1 as the closing point, and keep r plus 1 and the lengths in long long.
With two levels (how often each operation runs, then what the operations do), finish the prefix pass of the first level before you apply the second.
Reorder the array to maximise the total of fixed range-sum queries: that is, count how many queries cover each index with a difference array, then give the largest values to the most-covered indices

Choose one common target (a pair sum, a temperature, a level) and minimise the changes: that is, each item adds its cost on a few intervals of the target; build a difference array over the target and scan every candidate
Count triples (x, y, z) under an inequality: that is, for each x add +1 over the range of possible sums x plus y, then combine the sum counts with z in one scan

A process where each source is used up by consecutive consumers: that is, prefix sums plus binary search find where each source runs out, and a difference array records the range of consumers it served in full
Range updates without touching every cell: record where each one starts and stops in d (n plus 1 cells, all 0), then rebuild a once.
Add 3 to A from 1 to 4. First d of 1 plus-equals 3: from position 1 on, everything is 3 higher. d of 1 is now 3.
clips.script: Add 3 to eh from 1 to 4. First d of 1 plus-equals 3: from position 1 on, everything is 3 higher. d of 1 is now 3.

clips.text: Then d of 5 minus-equals 3: the increase stops after position 4. d of 5 is now minus 3. Two writes, however long the range.
Add 2 to A from 3 to 6. First d of 3 plus-equals 2: from position 3 on, everything is 2 higher. d of 3 is now 2.
clips.script: Add 2 to eh from 3 to 6. First d of 3 plus-equals 2: from position 3 on, everything is 2 higher. d of 3 is now 2.

clips.text: Then d of 7 minus-equals 2: the increase stops after position 6. d of 7 is now minus 2. Two writes, however long the range.
Add 1 to A from 0 to 2. First d of 0 plus-equals 1: from position 0 on, everything is 1 higher. d of 0 is now 1.
clips.script: Add 1 to eh from 0 to 2. First d of 0 plus-equals 1: from position 0 on, everything is 1 higher. d of 0 is now 1.

clips.text: Then d of 3 minus-equals 1: the increase stops after position 2. d of 3 is now 1. Two writes, however long the range.
Rebuild with a prefix sum over d: A of 0 is d of 0, so 1.
clips.script: Rebuild with a prefix sum over d: eh of 0 is d of 0, so 1.

clips.script: eh of 1 is eh of 0 plus d of 1, which is 1 plus 3, so 4.

clips.script: eh of 2 is eh of 1 plus d of 2, which is 4 plus 0, so 4.

clips.script: eh of 3 is eh of 2 plus d of 3, which is 4 plus 1, so 5.

clips.script: eh of 5 is eh of 4 plus d of 5, which is 5 minus 3, so 2.

clips.text: Done: 3 updates at O of 1 each, then one O of n pass. A of 1 got two updates: 3 plus 1 is 4.

clips.text: DP: states and transitions
Write a DP state as one sentence, add the small extra index the next step needs (last action, run length, time of day), and fill the table with take/skip or count-the-ways transitions.

A DP state is a sentence: "dp of i, s is the best answer for the first i positions, given that position i ended in situation s". The extra index s holds exactly what the next step needs to know about the past and nothing more: the last action, which row the last pick came from, the current run length, or the time of day mod h. The cost is (number of states) times (choices per state), so n positions with 3 extra states is O of n and n sleeps on an h-hour clock is O of n times h. Counting problems use the same table with plus instead of max, start from one way to build the empty prefix, and reduce modulo p after every addition.
Choices are made left to right (days, trees, students in a row) and each choice only restricts the next one or two
The rule mentions the previous step: not the same activity two days running, not the same row twice in a row, at most k in a row
Count the ways, modulo 10 to the 9 plus 7, to build something of length n from blocks or moves
A greedy rule fails on a small hand example, and the number of (position, extra state) pairs is at most about 10 to the 7

Initialising unreachable states to 0 when maximising. A length that cannot be cut exactly, or a day that cannot end in sport, must start at minus infinity (or a sentinel you skip) so it never feeds a later state.
Leaving a fact out of the state. If the transition at i depends on what happened at i minus 1 (which way a tree fell, which row the last student came from), that fact must be an index of dp.

Overflow and negative remainders: sums of 10 to the 5 heights of 10 to the 9 need long long, and (pre of b minus pre of A minus 1) mod MOD can be negative in C plus plus, so add MOD before the final mod.
clips.script: Overflow and negative remainders: sums of 10 to the 5 heights of 10 to the 9 need long long, and (pre of b minus pre of eh minus 1) mod MOD can be negative in C plus plus, so add MOD before the final mod.

clips.text: Deleting a value also deletes every v minus 1 and v plus 1, then group equal values, then run the no-two-adjacent take/skip DP over the value axis (house robber)
Count walks of length n on a small fixed graph: that is, DP over steps whose state is the current vertex, or a class of vertices that symmetry makes interchangeable
Count strings built from fixed-size blocks: that is, ways of i is ways of i minus 1 plus ways of i minus k, plus prefix sums when the question asks about a range of lengths
A schedule that keeps drifting around a clock: that is, the state is the time mod h, not the absolute time
Pick values, never two neighbours, to maximise the total. dp of i is the best you can do with the first i plus 1 values.
dp of 0: skip 5 and have 0, or take it and have 5.
dp of 0 is max(0, 5), so 5: take 5.
dp of 1: skip 1 and keep dp of 0 is 5, or take 1 alone, since its neighbour 5 must go: 1.
dp of 1 is max(5, 1), so 5: skip 1.
dp of 2: skip 3 and keep dp of 1 is 5, or take it on top of dp of 0 is 5: 5 plus 3 is 8.
dp of 2 is max(5, 8), so 8: take 3.
dp of 3: skip 8 and keep dp of 2 is 8, or take it on top of dp of 1 is 5: 5 plus 8 is 13.
dp of 3 is max(8, 13), so 13: take 8.
dp of 4: skip 2 and keep dp of 3 is 13, or take it on top of dp of 2 is 8: 8 plus 2 is 10.
dp of 4 is max(13, 10), so 13: skip 2.
dp of 5: skip 6 and keep dp of 4 is 13, or take it on top of dp of 3 is 13: 13 plus 6 is 19.
dp of 5 is max(13, 19), so 19: take 6.
Walk back: dp of 5 took 6, so it is in. Its neighbour can't be, so jump to dp of 3.
Walk back: dp of 3 took 8, so it is in. Its neighbour can't be, so jump to dp of 1.
Walk back: dp of 1 is dp of 0 skipped 1. Step to dp of 0.
Walk back: dp of 0 took 5, so it is in. Its neighbour can't be, so jump to the start.
Best total: 5 plus 8 plus 6 is 19. O of n time, and only the last two dp values are ever needed.
LIS, LDS and their disguises
Compute longest increasing, non-decreasing and decreasing subsequences in O of n log n, rebuild one, and recognise LIS behind problems about removing, nesting, crossing or colouring.

The longest increasing subsequence (LIS) is the largest set of elements you can keep, in their original order, so that they increase. The O of n squared DP dp of i is 1 plus max dp of j over j less than i with A of j less than A of i is fine up to n about 5000 and works for any "can follow" test, such as nesting in two dimensions; the O of n log n method keeps tails of k, the smallest last value of an increasing subsequence of length k plus 1, and places each A of i by binary search. The variants are small switches on this one routine: strict versus non-strict is lower bound versus upper bound, decreasing is LIS of the negated values, and by Dilworth's theorem the fewest non-decreasing subsequences that cover an array is its longest strictly decreasing subsequence (and the fewest non-increasing ones is the LIS).

The variants are small switches on this one routine: strict versus non-strict is lower bound versus upper bound, decreasing is LIS of the negated values, and by Dilworth's theorem the fewest non-decreasing subsequences that cover an array is its longest strictly decreasing subsequence (and the fewest non-increasing ones is the LIS).

clips.text: Keep, or remove, as many items as possible so that what is left is in order
Items are pairs such as (width, height) or (entry hole, exit hole), and one item fits inside, follows or crosses another
A graph whose edges join inverted pairs (a bigger value before a smaller one): its independent sets are increasing subsequences and its cliques are decreasing ones
The fewest groups, colours or passes such that each group on its own is sorted

Mixing up strict and non-strict: lower bound builds a strictly increasing subsequence, upper bound a non-decreasing one. "Remove the fewest so the rest is sorted" usually allows equal values, so it needs upper bound.
Treating tails as an actual subsequence. It only certifies the length; to rebuild one, store for each i the index that ended the previous length (par of i) and walk back from the end of the longest.

Sorting pairs by the first coordinate and running LIS on the second when equal first coordinates may not chain. Sort ties by the second coordinate descending, or compare both coordinates in an O of n squared DP.
Fewest items to remove or move so the rest is sorted: that is, n minus the longest non-decreasing subsequence
Nest envelopes, boxes or dolls: that is, sort by one dimension, then LIS on the other (equal first coordinates must not chain)
Largest group of pairwise crossing segments between two parallel lines: that is, longest decreasing subsequence of exit positions listed in entry order (pairwise non-crossing: that is, LIS)
Fewest colours so that each colour class is sorted: that is, length of the longest strictly decreasing subsequence (Dilworth)
tails of k holds the smallest value an increasing subsequence of length k can end with. Each new value binary-searches tails.
tails is empty: 3 starts a subsequence of length 1.
1: is the length-1 tail 3 less than 1? No: search this length and shorter.
The first tail at least 1 is the length-1 tail 3. Replace it: length 1 can now end lower, at 1.
8: is the length-1 tail 1 less than 8? Yes, so 8 can go after it: search longer lengths.
8 is bigger than every tail, so it extends length 1 (ending 1) to length 2.
2: is the length-2 tail 8 less than 2? No: search this length and shorter.
2: is the length-1 tail 1 less than 2? Yes, so 2 can go after it: search longer lengths.
The first tail at least 2 is the length-2 tail 8. Replace it: length 2 can now end lower, at 2.
5: is the length-2 tail 2 less than 5? Yes, so 5 can go after it: search longer lengths.
5 is bigger than every tail, so it extends length 2 (ending 2) to length 3.
9: is the length-2 tail 2 less than 9? Yes, so 9 can go after it: search longer lengths.
9: is the length-3 tail 5 less than 9? Yes, so 9 can go after it: search longer lengths.
9 is bigger than every tail, so it extends length 3 (ending 5) to length 4.
4: is the length-3 tail 5 less than 4? No: search this length and shorter.
4: is the length-2 tail 2 less than 4? Yes, so 4 can go after it: search longer lengths.
The first tail at least 4 is the length-3 tail 5. Replace it: length 3 can now end lower, at 4.
7: is the length-3 tail 4 less than 7? Yes, so 7 can go after it: search longer lengths.
7: is the length-4 tail 9 less than 7? No: search this length and shorter.
The first tail at least 7 is the length-4 tail 9. Replace it: length 4 can now end lower, at 7.
7 ended a length-4 subsequence after 4, the length-3 tail when 7 arrived. Step back to 4.
4 ended a length-3 subsequence after 2, the length-2 tail when 4 arrived. Step back to 2.
2 ended a length-2 subsequence after 1, the length-1 tail when 2 arrived. Step back to 1.
1 started its subsequence, so stop. Reading forwards: 1, 2, 4, 7.
LIS length 4: 1, 2, 4, 7. n binary searches: O of n log n. Use upper bound for non-decreasing.
LCS, edit distance and two-sequence DP
Set up dp of i, j over prefixes of two sequences to align, count, score or edit them, and spot the hidden second sequence when it is a reverse, a permutation order or a pattern automaton.

When a problem compares two sequences, let dp of i, j be the answer for the prefixes A from 0 up to i and b from 0 up to j. Each cell looks at three neighbours: drop the last item of a (i minus 1, j), drop the last item of b (i, j minus 1), or pair the two last items (i minus 1, j minus 1). That is O of nm time, and O of m memory with two rolling rows when you only need the value. Twists change what a cell stores (a count, a score, a piece counter, an automaton state), not the shape of the table.
clips.script: When a problem compares two sequences, let dp of i, j be the answer for the prefixes eh from 0 up to i and b from 0 up to j. Each cell looks at three neighbours: drop the last item of a (i minus 1, j), drop the last item of b (i, j minus 1), or pair the two last items (i minus 1, j minus 1). That is O of nm time, and O of m memory with two rolling rows when you only need the value. Twists change what a cell stores (a count, a score, a piece counter, an automaton state), not the shape of the table.

clips.text: Two strings or arrays of length up to about 5000, and the statement talks about subsequences, matching, aligning, merging or interleaving them.
Operations insert, delete and replace, or "fewest characters to change or remove so that A becomes B".
A score that rewards matched characters and penalises unmatched ones, often over substrings rather than whole strings.
Palindromes, or a process that grows outwards from a point: compare the sequence with its own reverse.

Off-by-one between table and string indices: with an (n plus 1) times (m plus 1) table, cell (i, j) compares A of i minus 1 with b of j minus 1, and row 0 and column 0 are the empty-prefix base cases (0 for LCS, i or j for edit distance).
clips.script: Off-by-one between table and string indices: with an (n plus 1) times (m plus 1) table, cell (i, j) compares eh of i minus 1 with b of j minus 1, and row 0 and column 0 are the empty-prefix base cases (0 for LCS, i or j for edit distance).

clips.text: Substring versus subsequence: for substrings a mismatch resets the cell (to 0 or minus infinity) instead of inheriting max(dp of i minus 1, j, dp of i, j minus 1), and "best over all substring pairs" is the maximum over every cell, not dp of n, m.
Memory: a 5000 times 5000 int table is 100 MB. Keep two rows when you only need the value, and the full table only when you must walk back to reconstruct the answer.
Fewest deletions from both strings to make them equal: that is, the size of A plus the size of b minus 2 times LCS(A, b).
clips.script: Fewest deletions from both strings to make them equal: that is, the size of eh plus the size of b minus 2 times LCS(eh, b).

clips.text: Fewest insertions to make a string a palindrome, or the longest palindromic subsequence: that is, LCS of the string and its reverse.

Longest common subsequence of several permutations: that is, a common subsequence is a chain in the order "x before y in every permutation", so it is a longest path in a DAG; with two permutations, relabel by positions and it becomes LIS.
Longest common subsequence that must avoid (or contain) a pattern P: that is, add a third index, the KMP automaton state: how much of P the chosen characters currently end with.
dp of i, j is the LCS of the first i letters of s (rows) and the first j of t (columns). Row 0 and column 0 are empty prefixes: 0.

Knapsack and subset sums
Recognise a knapsack under any wording, decide what the capacity dimension really measures, and use the right loop direction for zero-one, unbounded and bounded items.

A knapsack DP indexes by a small additive resource, dp of c is best value with c of it used, and adds items one at a time, each in O of C, for O of n times C overall. The real work is choosing that dimension: it can be weight, elapsed time, the number of items covered, the peak storage in use during a step, a small value when the weight is huge, or a sum shifted by an offset. Loop direction then controls how often an item counts: capacity downwards for zero-one, upwards for unbounded.
You pick a subset of items, each with a cost and a gain, under a total budget that is at most about 10⁵ or can be capped there.
"Can we make exactly S" or "which totals are reachable": subset-sum feasibility, often as a bitset.
One quantity is huge (up to 10⁹) and another is small (total at most 10⁵): index by the small one and store the best of the huge one.
A condition such as "ratio is k" or "the two sums are equal": rewrite it as a sum of per-item differences that must equal 0.
Wrong loop direction: sweeping capacity upwards in a zero-one knapsack lets one item be taken many times. With a negative weight the safe direction flips; when unsure, copy the row.

"At most c" versus "exactly c": all zeros means at most, minus infinity except dp of 0 is 0 means exactly. If you computed exactly, take the maximum over all c at most C (or make the table monotone) before reading the answer, otherwise a capacity that cannot be filled exactly looks impossible.
A capacity far larger than the items can use: k up to 10⁶ when the weights can only add up to 12n. Cap the capacity at the total weight before allocating the table.
Each paid item gives time to take t other items for free, pay as little as possible: that is, each paid item covers t plus 1 items; a min-cost knapsack whose capacity is "items covered", capped at n.

Items with a duration and a deadline, maximise the value finished in time: that is, sort by deadline (exchange argument), then a zero-one knapsack over elapsed time where an item fits only if its finish time is before its deadline.
Total taste divided by total calories must equal k: that is, weight A minus k times b per item, possibly negative; a knapsack over that sum with an offset, target exactly 0.
clips.script: Total taste divided by total calories must equal k: that is, weight eh minus k times b per item, possibly negative; a knapsack over that sum with an offset, target exactly 0.

clips.text: Grid DP, interval DP and choosing the state

Design DP states over grid cells, over segments dp of l, r filled by length, and over small tuples such as the last item on each line, and spot the reorder or delete problems that collapse into one of them.

On a grid, the best value at a cell depends only on the cells you could have come from, so one pass in row order solves a path problem in O of nm; running the same pass from other corners lets you glue path pieces together at a meeting cell. On a sequence that gets merged, deleted or folded in place, the answer for the segment l to r depends only on shorter segments inside it, so dp of l, r filled in order of increasing length gives O of n to the 2 states and usually O of n to the 3 time, which is why these problems have n at most 500. The real work is choosing the state: the smallest description of a partial solution that still decides every future move, such as the segment still on the table, the count of 2s so far, or the last item placed on each of three lines (UKIEPC 2025 Klaus); UKIEPC 2023 Clearing Space was a DP over points on a circle.
n at most 500 (or n at most 5000 with an O of n to the 2 DP) and an operation that removes or merges a contiguous block, after which the neighbours close up.
A grid walk with right/down moves where you optimise or test something about the path, or two walkers whose paths interact.
Questions about every substring or subarray: how many palindromes inside s from l to r, can A from l to r collapse into one element.
clips.script: Questions about every substring or subarray: how many palindromes inside s from l to r, can eh from l to r collapse into one element.

A 5000 times 5000 table of int is 100 MB and of long long is 200 MB. Store flags as bool or char and check the memory limit before choosing the type.

Bitmask DP and meet in the middle
Read n at most 20 (or n at most 40) as an invitation to enumerate subsets, and write dp of mask, dp of mask, last, submask loops, sum-over-subsets and meet-in-the-middle solutions.

When n is around 15 to 20, a set of chosen items fits in an int, and a DP indexed by that set replaces n! orderings with 2 to the n times n states, because the future depends only on which items are used and which one came last: dp of mask, last runs in O of 2 to the n times n to the 2. Splitting every mask into two disjoint parts costs O of 3 to the n in total with the submask loop, and sum over subsets (SOS) aggregates over all submasks of every mask in O of B times 2 to the B. When n is around 35 to 40, 2 to the n is too slow but 2 to the n over 2 is fine: enumerate each half on its own and combine the two lists by sorting and binary search (meet in the middle); UKIEPC 2023 Enchanted Fortress combined bitmasks with exactly this.
n at most 16, 18 or 20 with an ordering or a selection to optimise: 2 to the 20 times 20 about 2 times 10 to the 7, so the constraint itself is the hint.
n at most 35 or 40 with a subset to choose, where 2 to the n is hopeless but 2 to the n over 2 about 2 times 10 to the 5 to 10 to the 6 is not.
The cost of the next item depends only on the previous one (adjacent pairs, compatible neighbours, chains of transitions).
Values below 2 to the 20 to 2 to the 22 and a question about AND/OR relations against the whole array (is there a y with x and y is 0, how many elements are submasks of x).
Operator precedence: mask and 2 to the i is 0 parses as mask and ((2 to the i) is 0). Write (mask shifted right by i and 1) or bracket everything.
Memory: dp of 2 to the 20, 20 of long long is 160 MB. Use int when values allow, or store a boolean dp of mask, last as one bitmask of possible last items per mask.

The loop for (s is mask; s greater than 0; s is (s - 1) and mask) skips the empty submask; handle s is 0 separately when it matters, and never write s at least 0 as the condition, since (0 - 1) and mask brings you back to mask and the loop never ends.
Reorder songs, dishes or rows so that every adjacent pair is compatible or scores a bonus: that is, a Hamiltonian path, dp of mask, last over the items placed so far

Order matrix rows to maximise the minimum difference between neighbours in a column-by-column traversal: that is, precompute one cost per pair of rows, then a Hamiltonian-path DP with a fixed first row that maximises a minimum instead of a sum
For every x find an array element y with x and y is 0, which means y is a submask of the complement of x, so an SOS DP that stores one witness per mask answers all queries

Pick a subset of up to 35 numbers to maximise the sum modulo m: that is, split into halves, list the 2 to the 17 or 2 to the 18 subset sums of each, sort one list and binary search a partner for each sum in the other
dp of mask is cheapest way for the first popcount(mask) workers to cover the jobs in mask (bit j is job j). dp of 000 is 0, the rest start at infinity.
From 000 (0), worker 0 takes job 0: 0 plus 4 is 4 less than infinity, so dp of 001 is 4.
From 000 (0), worker 0 takes job 1: 0 plus 2 is 2 less than infinity, so dp of 010 is 2.
From 000 (0), worker 0 takes job 2: 0 plus 8 is 8 less than infinity, so dp of 100 is 8.
From 001 (4), worker 1 takes job 1: 4 plus 3 is 7 less than infinity, so dp of 011 is 7.

From 010 (2), worker 1 takes job 2: 2 plus 7 is 9 less than infinity, so dp of 110 is 9.
From 011 (6), worker 2 takes job 2: 6 plus 5 is 11 less than infinity, so dp of 111 is 11.

From 100 (8), worker 1 takes job 1: 8 plus 3 is 11 at least 9, so dp of 110 stays 9.
From 101 (11), worker 2 takes job 1: 11 plus 1 is 12 at least 11, so dp of 111 stays 11.
From 110 (9), worker 2 takes job 0: 9 plus 3 is 12 at least 11, so dp of 111 stays 11.
dp of 111 is 11 came from 011 (6): worker 2 took job 2 for 5.
dp of 011 is 6 came from 010 (2): worker 1 took job 0 for 4.
dp of 010 is 2 came from 000 (0): worker 0 took job 1 for 2.
Cheapest total 11: worker 0 on job 1, worker 1 on job 0, worker 2 on job 2. O of 2 to the n times n instead of n! orders.
DP with Fenwick and segment trees

Turn O of n squared transitions of the form "best or total over earlier items with a smaller key" into O of n log n with a Fenwick tree over compressed keys, count ordered pairs and chains, and write segment trees with custom merges and lazy range updates.

Many quadratic DPs have the transition dp of i is w of i plus best dp of j over j less than i with key of j less than key of i (or a sum instead of a best). Process the items in index order and keep a Fenwick tree indexed by the compressed key: only earlier items have been inserted, so j less than i holds automatically, key of j less than key of i becomes a prefix query, and the whole DP runs in O of n log n. A segment tree does the same for any associative merge (minimum, per-bit counts, a bracket summary), and lazy propagation adds range updates in O of log n each. UKIEPC 2024 Eradication Sort was an LIS-like DP sped up with a Fenwick tree, and UKIEPC 2023 History in Numbers needed a lazy segment tree.
An O of n squared DP whose transition takes the max or sum of dp of j over earlier j with a smaller (or larger) value, and n is 10 to the 5 to 10 to the 6.
Count pairs, triples or length-k chains of indices whose values are ordered: inversions, decreasing triples, increasing subsequences of length k.
Point or range updates interleaved with range questions (sum, minimum, or a summary that two halves can combine).
An update that changes a whole range at once (add v, xor x, assign) followed by range queries: lazy propagation.

Strict versus non-strict: when equal keys share a compressed rank, query rank minus 1 for "strictly smaller" and rank for "smaller or equal". Inserting dp of i before computing it lets i be its own predecessor.

Lazy propagation: push the pending tag to both children before recursing into them and recompute the node from its children afterwards. If a node's stored value already includes its own tag, applying the tag again on the way down double-counts it.

Overflow: counts of triples reach n cubed/6 and sums of 10 to the 5 values of 10 to the 12 need long long. If intermediate counts can pass 2 to the 63 while the final answer is guaranteed small, unsigned long long wraps mod 2 to the 64 and still produces the exact answer.

Stack cakes, boxes or envelopes so that each is strictly larger than the one below and maximise the total: that is, a weighted LIS, dp of i is vol i plus max dp of j over earlier strictly smaller volumes, one prefix-max Fenwick query per item (629D)

clips.text: DFS, components and cycles
Turn a statement into a graph, label its connected components in O of n plus m, and use the same traversal to detect cycles and 2-colour (bipartite) structure, on explicit graphs and on grids.

Name the vertices (people, cells, snow drifts) and the edges (friends, shared side, same row), then one O of n plus m traversal started from every unvisited vertex labels the connected components. The same pass can collect facts per component (size, edge count, degrees) and 2-colour it, which answers "is it a single cycle", "does it contain a cycle" and "can it be split into two sides" without a second algorithm. The hard part is usually building the graph: grids, points that share a coordinate and lists of group members are all graphs once you decide what the vertices and edges are.
Symmetric reachability questions: "can he get from any X to any Y", "how many users will hear the news", "how many separate regions": connected components.
A grid of cells with walls or colours and a question about areas, rooms or connected regions: flood fill, with cells as vertices and shared sides as edges.
"Split into two groups so that every edge goes across", "every edge joins an odd and an even number", "no two adjacent vertices get the same label": 2-colouring (bipartite check).
The question is whether some loop exists, or whether a component is a single ring: detect a non-parent visited neighbour during DFS, or compare edges with vertices per component.
Recursive DFS on 2 times 10 to the 5 vertices, or on a 500 times 500 grid whose empty cells form one long snake, can overflow the stack; use an explicit stack or BFS when the depth can be large.

With many test cases, allocate the adjacency lists and visited arrays for this test (size n) instead of clearing a global array of the maximum size, which is O of t times maxN when t is 3 times 10 to the 5.

In an undirected graph the edge back to the parent is not a cycle. Skip the parent (by edge id if multi-edges exist), or use the count rule: a component contains a cycle exactly when its edge count is at least its vertex count.

Fewest new objects or roads so that everything becomes mutually reachable: that is, number of components minus 1, since one new link can merge two components (217A: drifts sharing an x or y coordinate are adjacent).
Groups or cliques given as member lists: that is, link consecutive members of each list; k minus 1 path edges give the same components as the k(k minus 1) over 2 pairs (1167C).
Orient edges, assign parities or label vertices so that every edge joins two different kinds: that is, 2-colour the graph; it is possible exactly when there is no odd cycle (1144F, 1093D).
Remove k cells and keep the rest connected: that is, keep the first s minus k cells a search discovers (they form a tree), or remove DFS-tree leaves first (377A).

BFS, multi-source BFS and state graphs

Find fewest-move answers in O of V plus E with BFS: from one source or many, on the reversed graph, with zero-one move costs, and on graphs whose vertices are states (position plus whatever else matters) that you build from the statement.

BFS takes vertices out of the queue in order of distance, so when every move costs the same, the first time a vertex is reached is its shortest distance, in O of V plus E total. Three extensions cover most problems: start many sources at distance 0 to get "distance to the nearest of a set", run it on the reversed graph to get every vertex's distance to a target set in one pass, and push 0-cost moves to the front of a deque (0-1 BFS). The real modelling step is choosing the vertices: when the rules depend on more than your position (the direction you face, turns used, the previous city, the time), the vertex is the tuple of all of it.
"Minimum number of moves, clicks, steps or minutes" where every move costs the same: BFS, not DP or Dijkstra.
Many starting points spreading at once (fires, infections, shops), or "distance to the nearest X" for every cell: multi-source BFS.
A distance asked for every starting vertex but towards a fixed set of targets: reverse the edges and run one BFS from the targets.

Whether a move is allowed, or what it costs, depends on history (direction, turns used, previous city, time of day): BFS over states (position, extra info); if some moves are free and others cost 1, use 0-1 BFS.
Marking a vertex visited when it is popped instead of when it is pushed lets the queue hold many copies of it (up to O of E), which runs out of time or memory. Set dist when you push.

Count the states before coding: 10 to the 6 cells times 4 directions is fine, times 4 directions times 10 to the 3 times is not. Store a state as one integer id with a flat dist array, not a map of tuples.

Plain BFS (first visit is final) gives wrong distances once moves have different costs. zero-one costs need a deque (0-1 BFS) or Dijkstra; re-pushing improved vertices to the back of an ordinary queue is correct but can be very slow.
A device whose buttons change a number: that is, BFS over the numbers it can display, capped at the largest useful value (520B), or the same search run backwards from the target.
"For each i, the fewest jumps to any position with property P": that is, reverse every jump and run one multi-source BFS from all positions with P (1272E).
"Cheapest s different types of goods for every town" with only k at most 100 types: that is, k multi-source BFS passes, one per type, instead of n single-source ones (986A).

Forbidden triples of consecutive cities, a limit on turns or a timetable: that is, the vertex is (previous city, city), (cell, direction) or (place, time) (59E, 793B). UKIEPC 2023 Journey of Recovery searches such a time-expanded graph backwards from the destination.
BFS from S; cells are (row,column). A cell gets its distance the moment it is first reached, then waits in the queue (amber) to be expanded.

Dequeue (0,5) at distance 9. Enqueue (0,6) at distance 10. That reaches T, and in BFS its distance is already final: stop.
T is 10 steps from S. Following each cell's parent back from T gives a shortest path (green). Cells left in the queue never needed expanding.
Trees: DFS order, subtree DP and rerooting

Root a tree in O of n, use depth, subtree sizes and DFS order to answer subtree questions, write bottom-up DP on subtrees, reroot it to get an answer for every vertex, and find a diameter with two BFS passes.

Rooting the tree once gives every vertex a parent, a depth and a subtree (the vertex and everything below it). One DFS from the root visits the vertices in preorder; walking that order backwards finishes every child before its parent, so a DP over subtrees is a single O of n pass. A DFS finishes a subtree before it leaves it, so each subtree is a contiguous block of the preorder, order of tin v to tin of v plus size of v minus 1, which turns "everything below v" into an array range. When the statement wants an answer for every vertex as the root, compute it for one root and move the root across each edge with an O of 1 update (rerooting): O of n in total instead of O of n squared.
What the arrays mean
par of v: v's parent once the tree is rooted; the root has none ( minus 1).
depth of v: the number of edges from the root down to v (dep in the TRD version).
order: the vertices in DFS preorder, the order in which a DFS from the root first reaches them (in the TRD version, rootTree builds a BFS order and preorder() fills tin).
tin of v: the position of v in order, also called its entry time.
size of v: how many vertices are in v's subtree, v included (sub in the TRD version).
down of v: in a subtree DP, the answer for v's subtree on its own, filled children first.
ans of v: in rerooting, the answer with v as the root, filled parents first from ans of par v.
n vertices and n minus 1 edges, "connected and acyclic", or parents given as p i less than i: it is a tree, and once rooted every vertex has a well-defined subtree.
The value at a vertex depends only on what lies below it (counts, sums, the best choice among children): a subtree DP processed children-first.
"For every vertex v, if v were the root / capital / meeting point" or "choose v to maximise sum of dist(i, v) times A i": rerooting.
clips.script: "For every vertex v, if v were the root / capital / meeting point" or "choose v to maximise sum of dist(i, v) times eh i": rerooting.

clips.text: "Farthest pair", "longest path" or "pick vertices so their paths cover the most edges": the diameter, found by two BFS passes.

Recursive DFS on a path of 2 times 10 to the 5 vertices can overflow the stack, especially on Windows-based judges; use an explicit stack for the preorder and loop over it backwards for bottom-up passes.
Calling every degree-1 vertex a leaf also catches the root when it has a single child; a leaf is a non-root vertex with no children.

In the rerooting pass, the upward value for child v must use the parent's full answer with v's own contribution removed (for example ans of p minus max(0, down of v)), not down of p, which ignores everything above p. Distance sums like sum of dist times A i reach 10 to the 15 and need long long.

Choose the best centre for a weighted sum of distances: that is, compute the sum for root 1, then reroot: moving from p to its child v changes it by S minus 2 times sub(v), where S is the total of all the weights and sub(v) the total inside v's subtree (1092F). This is the "move to a neighbour with an O of 1 update" step in UKIEPC 2024 Jabber Network.

8 is a leaf: size of 8 is 1. Finished, so return to 5.
All of 5's children are finished: size of 5 is 1 plus size of 7 plus size of 8, which is 1 plus 1 plus 1, so 3.
All of 2's children are finished: size of 2 is 1 plus size of 4 plus size of 5, which is 1 plus 1 plus 3, so 5.

2's subtree 2, 4, 5, 7, 8 is order from 1 to 5: it starts at tin of 2 is 1 and has size of 2 is 5. DFS finishes a subtree before leaving it.
Subtrees nest as blocks: 5's is order from 3 to 5. So a query on the subtree of v is a range query on order of tin v to tin of v plus size of v minus 1.
DSU and minimum spanning trees

Maintain components under edge additions with union-find, answer threshold questions by adding edges offline in sorted order, and build minimum spanning trees with Kruskal or dense Prim, including the virtual-vertex trick for "build here or connect" costs.

A disjoint set union stores each component as a tree pointing to one representative; with path compression (here path halving) and union by size, find and unite take amortised O of α(n), effectively constant. Kruskal sorts the edges by weight and keeps an edge exactly when it joins two different components, which yields a minimum spanning tree in O of m log m. The same "add edges in sorted order" loop answers threshold questions offline: after all edges of weight at most q are in, the DSU holds exactly the components of the graph restricted to weight at most q.
Edges or "same group" relations are only ever added, and you need connectivity, component sizes or the number of components along the way.
"Connect everything at minimum total cost", or keep a subset of edges so everything stays connected and the total is minimal: a minimum spanning tree.
A threshold in the question, such as "using only edges of weight at most q" or "the largest edge on the path is at most q": sort the edges (and the queries) and union in increasing order.
Each object either pays its own fixed cost or links to another object that is already served: add a virtual vertex 0 with an edge (0, i) of weight c i.
Comparing p of a with p of b instead of find(A) with find(b), or merging A and b instead of their roots, silently corrupts the sets.
clips.script: Comparing p of a with p of b instead of find(eh) with find(b), or merging eh and b instead of their roots, silently corrupts the sets.

Materialising all n(n minus 1) over 2 edges of a dense graph costs memory and a large sort; for complete graphs with n about 2000 use O of n squared Prim with plain arrays, or prove that only O of n of the edges can ever be chosen.
Guests each want two shared items and you minimise the unhappy ones: that is, items are vertices, guests are edges, and the unhappy guests are the edges that close a cycle in the DSU (1209D).

Count pairs (u, v) whose path maximum is at most q: that is, union edges in increasing weight; merging components of sizes x and y adds x times y pairs, the same loop as Kruskal (1213G). UKIEPC 2025 Fell Walking fixed the minimum and then added edges in this Kruskal order.
Every city builds a power station for c i or wires to a powered neighbour: that is, an MST on n plus 1 vertices with a virtual power-station vertex (1245D).
A complete graph where connecting x and y costs A x plus A y: that is, only the star from the vertex with the smallest a can be in an MST, so the graph shrinks to O of n plus m edges (1095F).

Topological sort and DAG DP
Turn "x before y" constraints into a directed graph, find an order or prove none exists, and run DP along that order for longest paths, path counts and minimal layer numbers.

A directed graph can be listed so that every edge points forward exactly when it has no cycle, and Kahn's algorithm finds such an order in O of n plus m: repeatedly remove a vertex with no remaining incoming edges (reversed DFS finishing order works too). If some vertices are never removed, they lie on or behind a cycle, which is your IMPOSSIBLE or "infinite" case. Once you have the order, any DP whose transitions follow edges (longest or shortest path, number of paths, earliest layer) is one pass over it, because every predecessor of a vertex is final before the vertex is used.
The statement gives pairwise constraints: "a must come before b", "x is smaller than y", prerequisites, dependencies, or a list that is sorted under some unknown order.
You must answer "impossible", -1 or "infinite" when the requirements contradict each other or a walk could repeat forever: that is cycle detection.
The graph is promised to be acyclic ("no cyclic routes", "a task never depends on itself") and you want the best or the number of paths.
You must give items the smallest ranks, levels or values that respect a set of less than and is relations.

Not checking for a cycle: after Kahn's algorithm, compare the number of removed vertices with n. With DFS you need three colours (unvisited, on the stack, finished); a plain visited flag cannot tell a back edge from a harmless cross edge.

Running the DP in input order or vertex-number order, or starting Kahn's algorithm only from the source: start from every vertex with in-degree 0, or vertices fed by unreachable ones are never processed.
In "sorted under some order" problems, a word followed by its own proper prefix ("care" before "car") can never be sorted, and it produces no letter edge, so it must be checked separately.

Find an alphabet or ranking under which a given list is sorted: that is, compare neighbouring items; each first difference gives one edge "x before y", and any topological order of the letters is an answer.
How many passes, rounds or semesters until everything is done: that is, longest path in the dependency DAG, where an edge costs 1 when it forces a new pass and 0 otherwise.

Assign the smallest positive values satisfying A less than b and A is b: that is, merge the is groups with DSU, then a group's value is 1 plus the longest chain of less than edges ending at it; a cycle, or A less than inside one group, means no assignment.

clips.text: Dijkstra, Floyd–Warshall and state graphs
Compute single-source and all-pairs shortest paths, run Dijkstra over expanded states, and reuse a distance table to answer "what if this road changes" questions.

Dijkstra settles vertices in increasing order of distance with a priority queue, O of (n plus m) log m for non-negative weights, and it works on any graph you can describe, including expanded states such as (city, bike owned) or (vertex, riding or not). Floyd–Warshall gives all pairs in O of n cubed for n up to about 500, and its outer loop means something: after the pass for k, distances use only the first k vertices as stopovers, so vertices can be added one at a time. With all-pairs distances precomputed, "change one road", "add a road" or "visit these places in some order" questions turn into arithmetic or DP on the table.
Weighted edges with non-negative weights, and the question asks for the least total time, cost or distance from a start.
The cost of an edge depends on something you carry or have done (a bike, a horse, a ticket, fuel, discounts used): make that part of the vertex.
n is at most a few hundred and the question involves many pairs, or vertices and roads are added or removed over time: Floyd–Warshall or an O of n squared update per change.
You may change one road, or must visit a few special places: precompute distances from the relevant sources once, then combine table entries.

Missing the stale-entry check: without "if (d is not dist of v) continue" a vertex popped many times rescans its edges, which can blow up to O of n times m. Also use a min-heap (greater), not the default max-heap.
Overflow: 10 to the 5 edges of weight 10 to the 6 or more need long long, and an INF of LLONG MAX overflows as soon as you add to it; use LLONG MAX over 4 or skip INF entries.
Floyd–Warshall with k not as the outermost loop: the result is wrong but often still passes small tests.
Delete vertices one by one and report a sum over all pairs before each deletion: that is, reverse the order and add the vertices as the k of Floyd–Warshall.
Costs depend on an item picked up earlier (a bike, a horse, a coupon): that is, Dijkstra over states (vertex, item), with n times the number of item values states.
Two people travel and meet at a vertex as early as possible: that is, one Dijkstra from each start; meeting at v takes max(d1 of v, d2 of v), so minimise that over v.

Make one road free, or add one road, and minimise a sum of route lengths: that is, with all-pairs distances, route A to b becomes min(d of A, b, d of A, x plus c plus d of y, b, d of A, y plus c plus d of x, b) for road x to y of new length c.

clips.text: Binary lifting and LCA
Build jump tables up of k, v on trees and on "next" pointers to answer k-th ancestor, LCA, distance and path-maximum queries in O of log n, and count how many greedy steps lead from l to r.

Store for every vertex its 2 to the k-th ancestor, up of k, v is up of k minus 1, up k minus 1, v, which takes O of n log n to build. A jump of any length splits into its binary digits, and "climb as long as a condition still holds" becomes a descent from the largest power of two down, both O of log n. LCA lifts the deeper vertex to the same depth and then lifts both while their ancestors differ; keeping an aggregate (max edge, sum) next to each jump answers path queries the same way. The table works for any function next(x), not only parents: UKIEPC 2023 Fast Forward jumped through "next ad break" pointers exactly like this.
Many queries about paths between two vertices of a fixed tree: distances, whether a vertex lies on a path, the heaviest edge on a path.
For each vertex, "the highest ancestor that still satisfies X", where X is monotone along the root path (sums of positive weights, depths).
A greedy step "from position x go as far as possible" repeated many times, with many queries asking how many steps get from l to r.
Applying the same function k times with k up to 10 to the 9 or 10 to the 18: teleporters, permutations, successor graphs.
LOG must satisfy 2 to the LOG greater than the longest jump: depths up to 2 times 10 to the 5 minus 1 need LOG is 18, because 2 to the 17 is 131072 is too small.
Give the root (or a sentinel such as position n plus 1) a jump to itself. Otherwise up of k of the root reads garbage or index 0, and a "jump while the condition holds" loop walks off the tree.

Fill up of k, v only after the ancestors of v are complete: build in BFS order, or make k the outer loop over all vertices. A recursive DFS on a path of 2 times 10 to the 5 vertices can overflow the stack.

Minimum spanning tree that must contain a given edge: that is, MST weight minus the heaviest MST edge on the path between its endpoints plus its own weight; the path maximum comes from binary lifting (609E)
Fewest pieces or intervals covering l to r, over many queries: that is, a greedy "furthest reach" pointer next(x), and the answer is how often you apply it: jump tables over next (1516D, 1175E)

Is there one simple path through all these vertices?: that is, the deepest vertex and the deepest vertex off its root path are the ends; check dist(A, x) plus dist(x, b) is dist(A, b) with LCA (1702G2)

up of 2, 10 is up of 1, up 1, 10, which is up of 1, 8, so 1: two jumps of 2 make one of 4.

up of 2, 5 is up of 2, 10, so 1: a common ancestor, but maybe above the lowest one. Don't jump.
up of 1, 5 is 3 and up of 1, 10 is 8 differ, so the LCA is higher still: both jump 2.
up of 0, 3 is up of 0, 8, so 2: a common ancestor, but maybe above the lowest one. Don't jump.
3 and 8 are now children of the meeting point, so LCA is up of 0, 3, so 2.
LCA(7, 10) is 2. The path between them has depth of 7 plus depth of 10 minus 2 times depth of 2 is 8 edges.
Binary and ternary search on the answer
Turn "find the best value" into "is this value achievable?" and binary search the boundary, or ternary search a convex cost over one free parameter.

If testing one candidate answer is easy and feasibility is monotone (when x is achievable, so is every smaller x), binary search for the boundary: O of log range checks, each usually a greedy O of n pass, so O of n log range in total. On real numbers, run a fixed 60 to 100 halvings instead of looping until hi minus lo less than eps. When you instead choose one parameter (a position, a shift, a time) to minimise a cost that falls and then rises, such as a max or sum of convex pieces, ternary search discards a third of the interval per step; on integers, binary search on the sign of f(x plus 1) minus f(x) instead.
The statement asks for the largest or smallest value of something (cookies, time, radius, median) and a fixed candidate is easy to test, often greedily
Feasibility is monotone in the answer: more time, a larger radius or a lower target can only make the check easier
A real-valued output with tolerance 10 to the -6 together with a question of the form "can everything fit, or everyone meet, within T"
You pick one free parameter, such as a meeting point, a shift x or a final height, and the cost is a max or sum of the size of something minus parameter terms, which is convex in it

Mid rounding: with lo is mid you must take mid, which is lo plus (hi minus lo plus 1) over 2, or the loop never ends when hi is lo plus 1. Write the invariant (ok(lo) true, everything above hi false) before coding.

clips.text: Geometry: cross products, polygons and sweeps
Answer turn, side, intersection, area and inside/outside questions exactly with integer cross products, and process geometric events in sorted order with a sweep line.

Treat points as integer vectors. The cross product A times b is A x times b y minus A y times b x is twice the signed area of the triangle (0, A, b): its sign says whether b turns left or right of A, and almost everything else is built from it, including orientation tests, segment intersection, the shoelace area of a polygon, point in polygon and sorting by angle. With integer input these tests are exact in long long (or _ int128), so compare in integers and use floating point only for the printed answer. When objects interact along one axis, a sweep line sorts their start and end events and keeps the currently active objects in a set or Fenwick tree, turning O of n squared pair checks into roughly O of n log n.

The cross product eh times b is eh x times b y minus eh y times b x is twice the signed area of the triangle (0, eh, b): its sign says whether b turns left or right of eh, and almost everything else is built from it, including orientation tests, segment intersection, the shoelace area of a polygon, point in polygon and sorting by angle. With integer input these tests are exact in long long (or _ int128), so compare in integers and use floating point only for the printed answer. When objects interact along one axis, a sweep line sorts their start and end events and keeps the currently active objects in a set or Fenwick tree, turning O of n squared pair checks into roughly O of n log n.

Floating-point decisions: testing collinearity, "strictly inside" or ties with doubles and an epsilon gives WA on boundary tests. Keep every predicate in integers and convert only the final length or area.
Boundary cases: points on an edge, collinear consecutive vertices, segments that touch without crossing, and the wrap-around from the last vertex back to the first.

Convex hulls and the convex hull trick
Build a convex hull with the monotone chain, use it for containment and extreme-point questions, recognise hulls hiding in prefix sums and parabolas, and speed up DP with the convex hull trick.

The convex hull is the smallest convex polygon containing a point set. Andrew's monotone chain builds it in O of n log n: sort the points by x, then sweep once for the lower hull and once for the upper hull, popping the last point while it does not make a left turn. Many problems need only one chain: the upper hull consists of the lines through two points with no point above them, and the lower hull of prefix-sum points gives the smallest averages. The convex hull trick is the same idea for lines: the minimum of lines m times x plus c is a lower envelope, so a DP of the form dp of i is min j (dp of j plus m j times x i) runs in O of n instead of O of n squared when slopes and queries arrive in sorted order.
Questions about the outermost points of a set: the length of a fence around everything, which points can be extreme, whether one shape fits inside another
A DP transition dp of i is min or max over j of (dp of j plus f(j) times g(i)), a product of something about j and something about i, with n up to 10 to the 5 or 10 to the 6
Averages, slopes or rates built from prefix sums, such as choosing blocks with the smallest average
Curves like y is x squared plus bx plus c through pairs of points, which become straight lines after a change of variables

Collinear and duplicate points: decide whether points on hull edges belong to the hull (popping on at most 0, as in the template, drops them) and remove duplicates first; a hull of one or two points must still work.

Overflow in the convex hull trick: the test for a useless line multiplies an intercept difference (up to about 10 to the 18) by a slope difference, so use _ int128 or long double. Lines with equal slopes need explicit handling (keep the better intercept).

The monotone trick assumes sorted slopes and sorted queries. If queries are unsorted, binary search over the envelope instead of popping from the front; if slopes are unsorted too, use a Li Chao tree.

Repeatedly averaging segments to get the lexicographically smallest sequence: that is, the lower convex hull of the prefix-sum points (i, S i); each hull edge is a block whose value is the edge's slope
Parabolas y is x squared plus bx plus c with no point strictly above: that is, set Y is y minus x squared, which turns them into lines, and count upper-hull edges

Splitting time between activities with different rates to reach several targets: that is, the achievable rates form the convex hull of the activity vectors; find where the ray towards the target leaves it
dp of i is min j dp of j plus b j times A i with sorted A and b: that is, each j is a line with slope b j, and each step is a query on the lower envelope
