Every happy guest removes at least one new flavour and the first removes two, so a component with s flavours makes at most s minus 1 guests happy, and ordering the guests along a spanning tree achieves that. The sad guests are exactly the edges that are not needed for a spanning forest.
Unite x i and y i for each guest in input order and count the unite calls that return false (both flavours already connected). O of (n plus k) α(n).

Model flavours as vertices and guests as edges. In a component with s flavours, at most s minus 1 guests can be happy, and lining guests up in BFS order of a spanning tree makes exactly s minus 1 happy. So the minimum number of sad guests is k minus (n minus number of components) is the number of guests whose two flavours are already connected when processed. Count failed unions. O of (n plus k) α(n).
For one query q, delete every edge heavier than q. Which pairs (u, v) are counted, in terms of the pieces that remain?

A pair counts exactly when u and v are in the same component of the forest of edges with weight at most q, so the answer is sum of s(s minus 1) over 2 over those components. As q grows edges are only added, which is the Kruskal loop run offline: sort edges by weight and union them in that order.

Sort the edges; keep a running total and, when an edge joins components of sizes x and y, add x times y. Record the total after all edges of weight at most w for each w up to 2 times 10 to the 5 (or sort the queries with their indices) and answer by lookup. O of n log n plus m plus max w.

The largest edge on the u to v path is at most q iff u and v are connected using only edges of weight at most q. Sort the edges and sweep q upwards, uniting each edge once q reaches its weight; merging components of sizes x and y creates x times y new valid pairs. Store the running count per weight value and print the answers in input order. The count reaches n(n minus 1) over 2 about 2 times 10 to the 10, so use long long; with n is 1 there are no edges and every answer is 0.
Without special offers, any two vertices can be joined for A x plus A y. If you had to connect everything with only such edges, which vertex would you put at the centre?
clips.script: Without special offers, any two vertices can be joined for eh x plus eh y. If you had to connect everything with only such edges, which vertex would you put at the centre?

clips.text: Let r be the vertex with the smallest A. For any x, y the edge (x, y) at A x plus A y is the heaviest edge of the triangle x, y, r, so by the cycle property an MST never needs it. Only the n minus 1 star edges (r, i) plus the special offers matter, and the problem becomes a plain MST.
clips.script: Let r be the vertex with the smallest eh. For any x, y the edge (x, y) at eh x plus eh y is the heaviest edge of the triangle x, y, r, so by the cycle property an MST never needs it. Only the n minus 1 star edges (r, i) plus the special offers matter, and the problem becomes a plain MST.

clips.text: Find r is argmin A, build the edge list from the m special offers plus (r, i, A r plus A i) for every i is not r, and run Kruskal with a DSU, summing in long long. O of (n plus m) log(n plus m).
clips.script: Find r is argmin eh, build the edge list from the m special offers plus (r, i, eh r plus eh i) for every i is not r, and run Kruskal with a DSU, summing in long long. O of (n plus m) log(n plus m).

clips.text: Let r be the vertex with the smallest A. For a pair x, y, the cost A x plus A y is at least both A r plus A x and A r plus A y, so the direct edge is the heaviest in the triangle with r and can be dropped. Build the star from r together with all special offers, sort by cost and run Kruskal. A i and w go up to 10 to the 12 and the total to about 4 times 10 to the 17, so read and sum everything in long long. n is 1 prints 0.
clips.script: Let r be the vertex with the smallest eh. For a pair x, y, the cost eh x plus eh y is at least both eh r plus eh x and eh r plus eh y, so the direct edge is the heaviest in the triangle with r and can be dropped. Build the star from r together with all special offers, sort by cost and run Kruskal. eh i and w go up to 10 to the 12 and the total to about 4 times 10 to the 17, so read and sum everything in long long. n is 1 prints 0.

clips.text: Building a station costs c i and involves no other city. Can you make that option look like an edge, so that every decision is just "pick some edges"?

Add a virtual vertex 0, the power source, with an edge (0, i) of weight c i. A city has electricity iff it is connected to 0, so the cheapest plan is a minimum spanning tree on n plus 1 vertices: tree edges at 0 are stations, all other tree edges are wires.

The graph is complete with about 2 times 10 to the 6 edges, so run O of n squared Prim from vertex 0 with arrays best of and from of and no heap, computing (k i plus k j) times (the size of x i minus x j plus the size of y i minus y j) on the fly. Record from of v for each vertex you attach. O of n squared.

Vertex 0 stands for "has a power station" with edge weights c i; wires cost (k i plus k j) times the Manhattan distance. A plan is valid iff every city is connected to 0, so the optimum is an MST of this complete graph on n plus 1 vertices. Dense Prim repeatedly attaches the cheapest unattached vertex and relaxes all others; a vertex attached from 0 gets a station, any other attachment is a wire. Wire costs reach about 4 times 10 to the 15, so use long long. O of n squared time, O of n memory; Kruskal on all pairs also passes but is slower.
Kruskal would take the cheapest edges first. Which edges cost less than p, and which array value is responsible for an edge of weight A i?
clips.script: Kruskal would take the cheapest edges first. Which edges cost less than p, and which array value is responsible for an edge of weight eh i?

clips.text: An edge of weight A i joins j and k exactly when every element of A from j to k is a multiple of A i and A i lies inside, so A i reaches a contiguous run of multiples around position i. Run Kruskal by hand: process positions in increasing A i and greedily connect i to its neighbours along that run at cost A i per new connection.
clips.script: An edge of weight eh i joins j and k exactly when every element of eh from j to k is a multiple of eh i and eh i lies inside, so eh i reaches a contiguous run of multiples around position i. Run Kruskal by hand: process positions in increasing eh i and greedily connect i to its neighbours along that run at cost eh i per new connection.

clips.text: Sort positions by A. For each i with A i less than p, walk left and right while the next element is divisible by A i and the gap between it and its neighbour is not yet bridged, marking the gap and adding A i. Stop at a bridged gap; finally add p for every gap still unbridged. Each gap is bridged once, so the walks cost O of n after the O of n log n sort.
clips.script: Sort positions by eh. For each i with eh i less than p, walk left and right while the next element is divisible by eh i and the gap between it and its neighbour is not yet bridged, marking the gap and adding eh i. Stop at a bridged gap; finally add p for every gap still unbridged. Each gap is bridged once, so the walks cost O of n after the O of n log n sort.

clips.text: Components stay contiguous, so track which of the n minus 1 gaps (j, j plus 1) are bridged. In increasing order of A i, while A i less than p, extend from i to the left while A j mod A i is 0 and gap j is unbridged, bridging it for A i (the edge (j, i) exists because all of A from j to i are multiples of A i), then do the same to the right. Stopping at a bridged gap is safe because an earlier walk with a value at most A i got there first and anything further that A i could reach is already in that component. Every remaining gap costs p. Values with A i at least p are skipped since the adjacent p-edges are never worse. Sum in long long.
clips.script: Components stay contiguous, so track which of the n minus 1 gaps (j, j plus 1) are bridged. In increasing order of eh i, while eh i less than p, extend from i to the left while eh j mod eh i is 0 and gap j is unbridged, bridging it for eh i (the edge (j, i) exists because all of eh from j to i are multiples of eh i), then do the same to the right. Stopping at a bridged gap is safe because an earlier walk with a value at most eh i got there first and anything further that eh i could reach is already in that component. Every remaining gap costs p. Values with eh i at least p are skipped since the adjacent p-edges are never worse. Sum in long long.

clips.text: Two neighbouring names in a sorted list tell you something only at their first differing position. What does "rivest" before "shamir" say about the alphabet?

Each neighbouring pair gives at most one constraint "letter x comes before letter y". You need an order of the 26 letters that respects all of them, which is a topological order of a 26-vertex graph; a cycle in that graph means Impossible.

For each i, find the first position k where name of i and name of i plus 1 differ and add the edge name of i, k: that is, name of i plus 1, k. If there is no such position and name of i is the longer one, print Impossible at once. Run Kahn's algorithm on the letters: fewer than 26 removed means Impossible, otherwise print the removal order.

Only adjacent names need comparing, since lexicographic order is transitive. Each adjacent pair contributes the edge name of i, k: that is, name of i plus 1, k at its first differing position k; when one name is a prefix of the other there is no edge, but a longer name followed by its own prefix ("care" then "car") is Impossible under any alphabet, which is the case most wrong answers miss. Kahn's algorithm on the 26 letters then gives a valid alphabet, or stops early on a cycle. O of total length plus 26 squared.
When can the value be arbitrarily large? And once you rule that out, what kind of graph is left?

Any cycle (a self-loop counts) can be walked around forever, so its letters repeat without bound and the answer is -1. Otherwise the graph is a DAG, and the best path in a DAG is DP over a topological order. You do not know which letter wins, so track all 26.

Run Kahn's algorithm; if not all n nodes are removed, print -1. Keep dp of v, c is the most occurrences of letter c on a path ending at v: when v is removed, add 1 to dp of v, s v, then for each edge v to u set dp of u, c is max(dp of u, c, dp of v, c) for all c. The answer is the largest entry, O of 26 times (n plus m).

If the graph has a cycle the answer is -1; Kahn's algorithm detects it, including self-loops x to x, because those nodes never reach in-degree 0. In a DAG, fixing the letter c turns the question into a longest path that counts nodes labelled c, so dp of v, c for all 26 letters at once, filled in topological order, gives the answer in O of 26 times (n plus m) time and 26 times n ints of memory. Multiple edges and disconnected parts need no special handling.
There are two quantities: showplaces visited (to maximise) and time spent (at most T). Times go up to 10 to the 9, so they cannot be a DP index, but the number of showplaces is at most 5000.

Swap the roles: for each showplace v and count k, store the least time needed to stand at v having visited exactly k showplaces. The roads form a DAG, so this table fills in topological order, each road turning a k-showplace route into a (k plus 1)-showplace route.

Set dp of 1, 1 is 0. For v in topological order and each road v to u with time t, set dp of u, k plus 1 is min(dp of u, k plus 1, dp of v, k plus t) and record par of u, k plus 1 is v. The answer is the largest k with dp of n, k at most T; follow par back from (n, k) to print the route. O of n times (n plus m).

dp of v, k is least time to reach showplace v from 1 visiting k showplaces, filled in a topological order of the whole graph (start Kahn's algorithm from every in-degree-0 vertex, not only from 1; states unreachable from 1 just stay infinite). Relax dp of u, k plus 1 from dp of v, k plus t along every road and store the parent, then take the largest k with dp of n, k at most T and walk the parents back. The trap is memory: 5001 squared entries are 100 MB as int, so store times as int (compute the sum in 64 bits and keep it only if at most T) and parents as short to stay under 256 MB. Time O of n times (n plus m) about 5 times 10 to the 7.
Chapter i can be understood in the same reading as a required chapter j only if j appears earlier in the book. What happens when j greater than i?

Treat each requirement as an edge j to i that costs 0 if j less than i and 1 if j greater than i (you must wait for the next reading). The reading in which chapter i is understood is 1 plus the heaviest path ending at i, so the answer is a longest path in the dependency DAG, and a cycle of requirements means -1.

Run Kahn's algorithm on the edges j to i with pass of i is 1 for every chapter, relaxing pass of i is max(pass of i, pass of j plus (j greater than i? 1: 0)). If fewer than n chapters are removed print -1, otherwise print the largest pass. O of n plus sum of k per test.

Chapter i is understood in reading max over its requirements j of (pass of j plus j greater than i), or reading 1 if it has none: a requirement that sits later in the book is only understood after the reader has passed chapter i, so i waits one more reading. That is a longest path with zero-one weights, computed in topological order of the requirement graph; chapters on or behind a cycle are never understood, so print -1 if Kahn's algorithm does not remove all n. Simulating the readings directly is O of n squared in the worst case (the fifth sample stretched to n chapters needs n readings).
Fix a threshold X and allow only vertices with A i at most X. Can you decide quickly whether k minus 1 moves are possible? How does the answer change as X grows?
clips.script: Fix a threshold X and allow only vertices with eh i at most X. Can you decide quickly whether k minus 1 moves are possible? How does the answer change as X grows?

clips.text: If X works, every larger X works too, so binary search on X. For a fixed X the allowed vertices form a subgraph: if it contains a cycle the coin can move forever, and if it is a DAG the longest possible walk is its longest path, a DP in topological order.

Binary search over the sorted distinct values of A. check(X): run Kahn's algorithm on the vertices with A i at most X; if some allowed vertex is never removed there is a cycle, so return true; otherwise compute the longest path in vertices, len of u is max(len of u, len of v plus 1), and return max len at least k. If check(max A) fails print -1. O of (n plus m) log n.
clips.script: Binary search over the sorted distinct values of eh. check(X): run Kahn's algorithm on the vertices with eh i at most X; if some allowed vertex is never removed there is a cycle, so return true; otherwise compute the longest path in vertices, len of u is max(len of u, len of v plus 1), and return max len at least k. If check(max eh) fails print -1. O of (n plus m) log n.

clips.text: The answer is the smallest X for which the subgraph on vertices with A i at most X contains a walk through k vertices. That holds if the subgraph has a cycle (k is up to 10 to the 18, so only a cycle can give such long walks) or if its longest path has at least k vertices, and one Kahn pass with a longest-path DP answers both. The predicate is monotone in X, so binary search over the distinct a values costs O of (n plus m) log n. Keep k in 64 bits, and note that k is 1 needs just one vertex, so the answer is never -1 when n at least 1 and k is 1.
clips.script: The answer is the smallest X for which the subgraph on vertices with eh i at most X contains a walk through k vertices. That holds if the subgraph has a cycle (k is up to 10 to the 18, so only a cycle can give such long walks) or if its longest path has at least k vertices, and one Kahn pass with a longest-path DP answers both. The predicate is monotone in X, so binary search over the distinct a values costs O of (n plus m) log n. Keep k in 64 bits, and note that k is 1 needs just one vertex, so the answer is never -1 when n at least 1 and k is 1.

clips.text: Ignore the undirected edges for a moment. If the directed edges alone contain a cycle, can anything save you? And if they do not?

The directed edges must already be acyclic, otherwise the answer is NO. If they are, take one topological order of all n vertices: an edge pointing from an earlier vertex to a later one can never close a cycle, so every undirected edge can be pointed forward in that order.

Run Kahn's algorithm on the directed edges only, over all n vertices, and record pos of v. If not every vertex is removed print NO. Otherwise print directed edges unchanged and each undirected edge x to y as "x y" if pos of x less than pos of y, else "y x". O of n plus m.

Directing the undirected edges only adds edges, so if the directed part has a cycle the answer is NO. Otherwise take a topological order of the directed part and orient each undirected edge from the earlier endpoint to the later one; every edge now goes forward in one fixed order, so the result is acyclic. Kahn's algorithm gives the cycle test and the positions in O of n plus m. Reset the adjacency lists and in-degrees for each test case, and include vertices that touch only undirected edges in the order.
Dishes marked "=" must get the same number, so treat each group of equal dishes as a single item. What do the "<" and ">" entries become between groups?

After merging "=" groups with DSU, every "<" is a directed edge between groups, and the smallest valid numbers are longest-path layers: a group with nothing below it gets 1, any other group gets 1 plus the largest value below it. A cycle, or a "<" or ">" between two dishes of the same group, means No.

Union dish i with dish n plus j for each "=". For each "<" add the edge find(i): that is, find(n plus j) (">" the reverse), printing No if both ends share a group. Run Kahn's algorithm over the group roots with val is 1 at sources and val of u is max(val of u, val of v plus 1); if not every root is removed print No, else print val of find(x) for each dish. O of nm.

Collapse equal dishes with DSU over all n plus m dishes, then build the "strictly better" graph between groups (up to 10 to the 6 edges). An evaluation exists exactly when no "<" or ">" lies inside a group and that graph is acyclic. Giving each group 1 plus the longest chain of groups below it is valid and makes every value individually as small as possible (a chain of L groups needs L distinct values), so the maximum is minimal too; it is a longest-path DP in topological order. When checking that Kahn's algorithm removed everything, count only DSU roots, not all n plus m dishes.
Deleting vertices is awkward. What if you read the deletions backwards, so the graph grows instead of shrinking?

In reverse, vertices are added one at a time, which is exactly what the outer loop of Floyd–Warshall does: after relaxing through a set S of vertices, d of i, j is the shortest i to j path whose stopovers all lie in S. So use x n, x_(n minus 1), …, x 1 as the successive k.

For step is n down to 1: let k is x step and set d of i, j is min(d of i, j, d of i, k plus d of k, j) for all i, j (all n vertices, not only the added ones). The answer before deletion step is the sum of d of i, j over added i and j. O of n cubed in total, with 64-bit sums.

Reverse the deletions so vertices are added. Keep the full n times n matrix and relax every pair through each newly added vertex k; after adding a set S, d of i, j is the shortest path using only stopovers from S, which for i, j in S is the distance in the remaining graph. Sum over pairs in S for that step and print the answers in the original order. Relaxing only pairs inside S is the common bug: a later vertex's routes through earlier ones are then never formed. O of n cubed about 1.25 times 10 to the 8 simple operations, and sums up to about 2.5 times 10 to the 10 need long long.
Once Slavic owns a bike, he never needs a slower one. So at any moment, which single number captures everything that matters about the bikes he has bought?

Only the slowness of the best bike owned so far matters, and it takes at most 1000 values. Put it in the vertex: Dijkstra on states (city, best slowness), a graph with n times 1000 vertices, because the fastest arrival at a city may carry a worse bike than a slightly slower arrival.

Start at (1, s 1) with time 0. From (v, b), a road v to u of length w leads to (u, min(b, s u)) at cost w times b (buying the bike at u is free and never hurts). The answer is the first popped state with city n. Use 64-bit times; O of 1000 times (n plus m) log.

Keep the slowness b of the fastest bike bought so far in the state; buying is free, so arriving at u always moves to (u, min(b, s u)). Dijkstra over the n times 1000 states with edge cost w times b gives the minimum, and the first state with city n taken from the heap is the answer. Times reach about 10 to the 11, so use long long. Dijkstra on cities alone is wrong because it keeps only the fastest arrival at each city and forgets that another arrival might carry a better bike.
Either of them may wait, so meeting at vertex v takes as long as the later of the two arrivals there. What do you need to know about each vertex?

Compute each traveller's earliest arrival at every vertex separately; the answer is the minimum over v of max(dM of v, dR of v). Each traveller is a single-source shortest path whose state also says whether they are riding, because riding halves every later edge.

Run Dijkstra twice (from 1 and from n) over states (v, riding) with riding ∈ 0, 1: at a horse vertex, (v, 0): that is, (v, 1) costs 0; an edge costs w on foot and w over 2 when riding. Let d of v be the smaller of the two states, then print min over v of max(d1 of v, dn of v), or minus 1 if it is infinite. O of (n plus m) log n.

Because waiting is allowed, the earliest meeting at v is max(d1 of v, dn of v), where each d is that traveller's own fastest arrival. Each is a Dijkstra on 2n states (vertex, mounted) with a free move onto a horse at horse vertices and halved edge costs once mounted (all w are even, so w over 2 is exact). The minimum over all v covers every meeting point. Reset everything between test cases and print minus 1 when 1 and n are disconnected.
This is the plain single-source problem. Besides the distances, what must you store to print the path itself?

Dijkstra with a binary heap is O of (n plus m) log n for non-negative weights. Recording, for each vertex, the vertex its distance last improved from gives the shortest-path tree, and the path to n is read off it backwards.

Keep dist as long long (10 to the 5 edges of weight 10 to the 6) and set par of u is v whenever dist of u improves through v. Skip heap entries whose distance is larger than dist of v. If dist of n is infinite print minus 1, else follow par from n back to 1, reverse, and print.

Standard Dijkstra from vertex 1 with a min-heap of (distance, vertex), the stale-entry check, and a predecessor stored on each improvement; reconstruct the path from n by following predecessors and reversing. Distances can reach 10 to the 11, so int overflows. Loops and multiple edges need nothing special. The usual failures are int distances and dropping the stale check, which on dense multi-edge tests rescans the same vertices many times.
You already have every shortest distance. When a new road A to b of length c opens, how can a new shortest path between cities i and j use it?
clips.script: You already have every shortest distance. When a new road eh to b of length c opens, how can a new shortest path between cities i and j use it?

clips.text: A new shortest path uses the new road at most once, in one of two directions, and the parts before and after it are old shortest paths. So each road needs one O of n squared relaxation pass through it, the same step Floyd–Warshall does for a single k, not a full rerun.

For each road: if c less than d of A, b, set d of i, j is min(d of i, j, d of i, A plus c plus d of b, j, d of i, b plus c plus d of A, j) for all i, j. Then print the sum of d of i, j over i less than j in 64 bits. O of k times n squared.
clips.script: For each road: if c less than d of eh, b, set d of i, j is min(d of i, j, d of i, eh plus c plus d of b, j, d of i, b plus c plus d of eh, j) for all i, j. Then print the sum of d of i, j over i less than j in 64 bits. O of k times n squared.

clips.text: Keep the distance matrix up to date. A path that uses the new road (A, b, c) has the form i to A to b to j or i to b to A to j with old shortest paths around the road, so one O of n squared pass with that formula fixes every pair; updating in place is safe because every value written is the length of a real path. Equivalently, set d of A, b is d of b, A, which is c and run the Floyd–Warshall step with k is A and then k is b. The sum over unordered pairs can exceed 2 to the 31, so use long long; total O of k times n squared about 2.7 times 10 to the 7.
clips.script: Keep the distance matrix up to date. A path that uses the new road (eh, b, c) has the form i to eh to b to j or i to b to eh to j with old shortest paths around the road, so one O of n squared pass with that formula fixes every pair; updating in place is safe because every value written is the length of a real path. Equivalently, set d of eh, b is d of b, eh, which is c and run the Floyd–Warshall step with k is eh and then k is b. The sum over unordered pairs can exceed 2 to the 31, so use long long; total O of k times n squared about 2.7 times 10 to the 7.

clips.text: In a shortest-path tree each vertex other than u has exactly one parent edge. Which edges are allowed to be that parent edge?

An edge (x, v, w) can be v's parent edge exactly when dist of x plus w is dist of v (a tight edge). Any choice of one tight edge per vertex forms a valid tree, because tight edges always come from strictly closer vertices, so the vertices can be decided independently and a greedy choice is optimal.

Run Dijkstra from u. For each vertex v is not u, pick the tight edge into v with the smallest weight; you can do this inside the relaxation by also replacing the parent edge when the distance ties and the new edge is lighter. Sum those weights and print their indices. O of (n plus m) log n with 64-bit distances.

Every shortest-path tree chooses, for each v is not u, one incoming edge with dist of x plus w is dist of v, and every such choice is a tree (weights are positive, so following parents strictly decreases dist and ends at u). The total weight is the sum of the chosen edges, so take the lightest tight edge for each vertex independently. In Dijkstra, update the parent edge on a strict improvement and also on a tie with a lighter edge. Distances reach 3 times 10 to the 14, and n is 1 must print 0 and an empty edge list.
There are only m at most 1000 roads to try and k at most 1000 routes. If you knew every pairwise distance, how fast could you evaluate one choice of free road?

Precompute all-pairs shortest paths once. Making road x to y free only helps a route A to b that crosses it, and then the route costs d of A, x plus d of y, b or d of A, y plus d of x, b with the old distances, so each (road, route) pair is O of 1.
clips.script: Precompute all-pairs shortest paths once. Making road x to y free only helps a route eh to b that crosses it, and then the route costs d of eh, x plus d of y, b or d of eh, y plus d of x, b with the old distances, so each (road, route) pair is O of 1.

clips.text: n is 1000 is too large for Floyd–Warshall, but the graph is sparse, so run Dijkstra from every district: O of n times m log n. Then for each road (x, y) compute the total sum of min(d of A, b, d of A, x plus d of y, b, d of A, y plus d of x, b) over the routes, and print the smallest total. O of n times m log n plus m times k.
clips.script: n is 1000 is too large for Floyd–Warshall, but the graph is sparse, so run Dijkstra from every district: O of n times m log n. Then for each road (x, y) compute the total sum of min(d of eh, b, d of eh, x plus d of y, b, d of eh, y plus d of x, b) over the routes, and print the smallest total. O of n times m log n plus m times k.

clips.text: After zeroing road x to y, a route A to b costs the minimum of its old distance and the two ways of crossing the free road, where the parts before and after the road are old shortest paths (a shortest route never needs the free road twice). Build the distance table with n Dijkstra runs, about 10 to the 7 operations, since Floyd–Warshall at n is 1000 is 10 to the 9. Then try every road against every route in O of m times k and take the minimum; zeroing a road never makes a route longer, so no separate "change nothing" case is needed.
clips.script: After zeroing road x to y, a route eh to b costs the minimum of its old distance and the two ways of crossing the free road, where the parts before and after the road are old shortest paths (a shortest route never needs the free road twice). Build the distance table with n Dijkstra runs, about 10 to the 7 operations, since Floyd–Warshall at n is 1000 is 10 to the 9. Then try every road against every route in O of m times k and take the minimum; zeroing a road never makes a route longer, so no separate "change nothing" case is needed.

clips.text: Along the path from the root to i, the b-sums of the prefixes only grow, because every b j at least 1. What shape does the set of prefixes with b-sum at most A i have?
clips.script: Along the path from the root to i, the b-sums of the prefixes only grow, because every b j at least 1. What shape does the set of prefixes with b-sum at most eh i have?

clips.text: Those prefixes end at exactly the root-path vertices u with B u at most A i, and they form the top part of the path. So r i is the depth of the deepest ancestor u of i with B u at most A i: a "climb while the condition fails" query, which binary lifting answers in O of log n.
clips.script: Those prefixes end at exactly the root-path vertices u with B u at most eh i, and they form the top part of the path. So r i is the depth of the deepest ancestor u of i with B u at most eh i: a "climb while the condition fails" query, which binary lifting answers in O of log n.

clips.text: Compute A, B and depth for all vertices in BFS order from vertex 1 (a parent can have a larger label than its child) and build up of k, v. For i: if B i at most A i then r i is depth i; otherwise jump by decreasing powers of two while the landing vertex still has B greater than A i, step once more to the parent and print its depth. O of n log n.
clips.script: Compute eh, B and depth for all vertices in BFS order from vertex 1 (a parent can have a larger label than its child) and build up of k, v. For i: if B i at most eh i then r i is depth i; otherwise jump by decreasing powers of two while the landing vertex still has B greater than eh i, step once more to the parent and print its depth. O of n log n.

clips.text: Let A v and B v be the a-sum and b-sum from the root to v. Since every b at least 1, B strictly increases down the path, so the prefixes with b-sum at most A i form a top part of the root-to-i path and r i is the depth of its deepest vertex. Find that vertex by lifting from i with decreasing powers of two while the landing vertex still has B greater than A i, then take one parent step; the root has B is 0 and points to itself, so the walk never leaves the tree. Root the tree with BFS because p j may exceed j, and keep the sums in long long. Keeping the B values of the current DFS path in an array and binary searching it is an equivalent O of n log n solution.
clips.script: Let eh v and B v be the a-sum and b-sum from the root to v. Since every b at least 1, B strictly increases down the path, so the prefixes with b-sum at most eh i form a top part of the root-to-i path and r i is the depth of its deepest vertex. Find that vertex by lifting from i with decreasing powers of two while the landing vertex still has B greater than eh i, then take one parent step; the root has B is 0 and points to itself, so the walk never leaves the tree. Root the tree with BFS because p j may exceed j, and keep the sums in long long. Keeping the B values of the current DFS path in an array and binary searching it is an equivalent O of n log n solution.

clips.text: A query vertex may be on the path or next to it. If v is next to a root-to-u path without being on it, which neighbour of v must be on the path? Can you swap each query vertex for one vertex that is certainly on the path?

Replacing every query vertex by its parent (the root stays itself) loses nothing. The condition becomes "all these vertices lie on one root-to-u path", that is, each of them is an ancestor of the deepest one. Ancestor tests are the building block of LCA.

Precompute parent, depth and DFS entry and exit times tin/tout. Per query map each v to parent(v), pick the deepest result w, and check tin of x at most tin of w and tout of w at most tout of x for every x (or lca(x, w) is x). O of n plus sum of k, or O of sum of k log n with binary-lifting LCA.

If v is within distance 1 of a root-to-u path, then parent(v) is on that path: if v is on it, so is its parent, and if v hangs off it, the path vertex next to v must be its parent, since a path through a child of v would pass through v. Conversely, parent(v) on the path puts v within distance 1. So replace each vertex by its parent, take the deepest result w, and answer YES exactly when every replaced vertex is an ancestor of w. Test ancestry in O of 1 with tin/tout from one iterative DFS, or with binary-lifting LCA, and keep the root mapped to itself.
Each pair of fools adds 1 to every road on one tree path, and walking each path edge by edge is O of n times k. Is there a tree version of "add 1 to a range in O of 1, read everything at the end"?

Root the tree. The path A to b climbs from A to lca(A, b) and descends to b. Put +1 on A and on b and minus 2 on their LCA; then the number of paths using the road from v to its parent is the sum of these marks over the subtree of v. All you need per pair is one LCA query, which binary lifting answers in O of log n.
clips.script: Root the tree. The path eh to b climbs from eh to lca(eh, b) and descends to b. Put +1 on eh and on b and minus 2 on their LCA; then the number of paths using the road from v to its parent is the sum of these marks over the subtree of v. All you need per pair is one LCA query, which binary lifting answers in O of log n.

clips.text: Build depths and up of k, v with a BFS from city 1, place the three marks for each pair, then add every vertex's total into its parent in reverse BFS order. For road i print the total of whichever endpoint is deeper. O of (n plus k) log n.

This is a difference array on a tree: for each pair (A, b) do cnt of a plus-equals 1, cnt of b plus-equals 1, cnt of lca(A, b) minus-equals 2. After subtree sums, the value at v counts exactly the paths with one end inside the subtree of v and the other outside, which are the paths using the road (v, parent(v)). LCA by binary lifting makes this O of (n plus k) log n. Print in input order by mapping each road to its deeper endpoint, and accumulate in reverse BFS order rather than with recursion, which can overflow the stack on a path-shaped tree.
clips.script: This is a difference array on a tree: for each pair (eh, b) do cnt of a plus-equals 1, cnt of b plus-equals 1, cnt of lca(eh, b) minus-equals 2. After subtree sums, the value at v counts exactly the paths with one end inside the subtree of v and the other outside, which are the paths using the road (v, parent(v)). LCA by binary lifting makes this O of (n plus k) log n. Print in input order by mapping each road to its deeper endpoint, and accumulate in reverse BFS order rather than with recursion, which can overflow the stack on a path-shaped tree.

clips.text: Fix the controlled vertex u and walk up its ancestors v. dist(v, u) only grows as v moves up. Which ancestors control u, then?

The controllers of u form a contiguous run of ancestors: from parent(u) up to the highest ancestor x with D u minus D x at most A u, where D is the weighted depth. Find x with binary lifting (jump while the condition still holds), then add 1 to every vertex on the vertical path parent(u) … x.
clips.script: The controllers of u form a contiguous run of ancestors: from parent(u) up to the highest ancestor x with D u minus D x at most eh u, where D is the weighted depth. Find x with binary lifting (jump while the condition still holds), then add 1 to every vertex on the vertical path parent(u) … x.

clips.text: Adding 1 along a vertical path is a tree difference array: mark of parent(u) plus-equals 1 and mark of parent(x) minus-equals 1 when x is not the root. The answer for v is the sum of marks in its subtree, accumulated in reverse BFS order. O of n log n.

Let D be the weighted depth. u is controlled by the proper ancestors v with D u minus D v at most A u, and since D decreases going up, they form a run from parent(u) up to a highest vertex x. Find x by lifting from u with decreasing powers of two while D u minus D target at most A u, skip u if not even its parent qualifies, and record +1 at parent(u) and minus 1 at parent(x). Subtree sums of these marks give every vertex's count, O of n log n in total. D reaches 2 times 10 to the 14, so use long long, and fill the tables in BFS order from vertex 1.
clips.script: Let D be the weighted depth. u is controlled by the proper ancestors v with D u minus D v at most eh u, and since D decreases going up, they form a run from parent(u) up to a highest vertex x. Find x by lifting from u with decreasing powers of two while D u minus D target at most eh u, skip u if not even its parent qualifies, and record +1 at parent(u) and minus 1 at parent(x). Subtree sums of these marks give every vertex's count, O of n log n in total. D reaches 2 times 10 to the 14, so use long long, and fill the tables in BFS order from vertex 1.

clips.text: If the set lies on one simple path, you can shorten the path so that it starts and ends at vertices of the set. Which vertex of the set is certainly one of the two ends?

The deepest vertex A is an end. The other end b is the deepest vertex that is not an ancestor of A; if every vertex is an ancestor of A, they all lie on A's root path and the answer is YES. Otherwise x lies on the path A to b exactly when dist(A, x) plus dist(x, b) is dist(A, b), and LCA gives distances.
clips.script: The deepest vertex eh is an end. The other end b is the deepest vertex that is not an ancestor of eh; if every vertex is an ancestor of eh, they all lie on eh's root path and the answer is YES. Otherwise x lies on the path eh to b exactly when dist(eh, x) plus dist(x, b) is dist(eh, b), and LCA gives distances.

clips.text: Precompute depths and binary lifting tables. Per query: A is deepest vertex, b is deepest x with lca(A, x) is not x, then check the distance equality for every x in the set. O of (n plus sum of k) log n.
clips.script: Precompute depths and binary lifting tables. Per query: eh is deepest vertex, b is deepest x with lca(eh, x) is not x, then check the distance equality for every x in the set. O of (n plus sum of k) log n.

clips.text: Take A is the deepest vertex of the set; if the set is passable, A is an end of the covering path. The vertices that are not ancestors of a (lca(A, x) is not x) all lie on the other branch, so the deepest of them is the other end b; if there are none, the whole set lies on the root path of A and the answer is YES. Otherwise check dist(A, x) plus dist(x, b) is dist(A, b) for every x, with dist from depths and binary-lifting LCA. O of (n plus sum of k) log n; k is 1 and n is 1 are valid inputs and must print YES.
clips.script: Take eh is the deepest vertex of the set; if the set is passable, eh is an end of the covering path. The vertices that are not ancestors of a (lca(eh, x) is not x) all lie on the other branch, so the deepest of them is the other end b; if there are none, the whole set lies on the root path of eh and the answer is YES. Otherwise check dist(eh, x) plus dist(x, b) is dist(eh, b) for every x, with dist from depths and binary-lifting LCA. O of (n plus sum of k) log n; k is 1 and n is 1 are valid inputs and must print YES.

clips.text: Start from one minimum spanning tree T. If an edge (u, v) outside T must be included, adding it closes exactly one cycle. Which edge of that cycle should you drop?

Drop the heaviest edge on the tree path between u and v, so the answer is W(T) minus maxOnPath(u, v) plus w; for an edge of T the path is the edge itself and the formula gives W(T). So the task is path-maximum queries on a fixed tree, which binary lifting answers by storing the heaviest edge next to each jump.

Run Kruskal for T. Root T and store up of k, v together with mx of k, v, the heaviest edge on the 2 to the k edges above v: mx of k, v is max(mx of k minus 1, v, mx of k minus 1, up k minus 1, v). For each input edge lift u and v to their LCA, taking the max over every jump used. O of m log m plus (n plus m) log n.

Build an MST with Kruskal and let W be its weight. Forcing edge (u, v, w) into the tree means removing one tree edge from the cycle it closes, and the best choice is the heaviest edge on the tree path u to v, giving W minus maxPath(u, v) plus w (this also yields W for the tree edges). Answer each path maximum with binary lifting that stores, beside each 2 to the k jump, the heaviest edge it covers, and combine those maxima during the LCA climb from both ends. O of m log m plus (n plus m) log n; W reaches 2 times 10 to the 14, so it must be long long.
When is the product of a group equal to its LCM? Think about primes. Then, for a single query, is cutting greedily from left to right optimal?

Product is LCM means no prime divides two elements of the group: they are pairwise coprime. Greedy is optimal, so from a start i the piece extends to just before go(i), the first index that cannot join it. The answer is how many times you apply go from l before passing r: jumping along a "next" pointer, which binary lifting makes O of log n per query.

Compute go from right to left: go(i) is min(go(i plus 1), the next index after i that contains a prime factor of A i), using a smallest-prime-factor sieve and a "next occurrence" array per prime, with go(n plus 1) is n plus 1. Build up of k, i. Per query, from x is l jump by 2 to the k while up of k, x at most r and count the steps; the answer is that count plus 1. O of (n plus q) log n.
clips.script: Compute go from right to left: go(i) is min(go(i plus 1), the next index after i that contains a prime factor of eh i), using a smallest-prime-factor sieve and a "next occurrence" array per prime, with go(n plus 1) is n plus 1. Build up of k, i. Per query, from x is l jump by 2 to the k while up of k, x at most r and count the steps; the answer is that count plus 1. O of (n plus q) log n.

clips.text: A group has product equal to its LCM exactly when its elements are pairwise coprime. From a start i the greedy takes the longest valid piece, which ends just before go(i) is min(go(i plus 1), the next index after i sharing a prime with A i); the min with go(i plus 1) is needed because a valid piece starting at i stays valid without A i. A query is then "how many go-steps from l until the position exceeds r", answered with binary lifting on go by jumping while the target is at most r and adding 1 for the last piece. Factorise with an SPF sieve up to 10 to the 5 and make n plus 1 a sentinel that points to itself.
clips.script: A group has product equal to its LCM exactly when its elements are pairwise coprime. From a start i the greedy takes the longest valid piece, which ends just before go(i) is min(go(i plus 1), the next index after i sharing a prime with eh i); the min with go(i plus 1) is needed because a valid piece starting at i stays valid without eh i. A query is then "how many go-steps from l until the position exceeds r", answered with binary lifting on go by jumping while the target is at most r and adding 1 for the last piece. Factorise with an SPF sieve up to 10 to the 5 and make n plus 1 a sentinel that points to itself.

clips.text: For one query, think greedily: x to cur is already covered. Which interval should you take next?

Take the interval with l at most cur that reaches furthest right: next(cur) is max(cur, maxr: l at most cur). The answer is the number of applications of next needed to reach y, and next is one fixed function on the coordinates 0 to 5 times 10 to the 5, so binary lifting counts the steps in O of log C.

Store the best r for each left end, take prefix maxima so that next(x) is max(x, prefix max at x), and set up of k, x is up of k minus 1, up k minus 1, x. Per query jump by 2 to the k while up of k, x less than y and add 2 to the k; then answer count plus 1 if next(x) at least y, otherwise minus 1. O of (C plus m) log C with C is 5 times 10 to the 5.

Greedy covering: with x to cur covered, take the interval starting at or before cur with the largest right end. Define next(c) is max(c, largest r over intervals with l at most c) for every coordinate using a prefix maximum, and build jump tables over next. For a query climb from x by powers of two while the landing point is still less than y; then one more step must reach y, otherwise there is a gap and the answer is minus 1 (a stuck point has next(c) is c, which the jumps preserve). The table has 19 levels of 5 times 10 to the 5 plus 1 ints, about 38 MB, which fits.
Sort the array first. Raising an element to the left of the median can never raise the median, so which elements matter? For a target median M, how many operations does it take?
Whether median M is reachable is monotone: if M costs at most k operations, so does every smaller M. So binary search on M with a cost check instead of looking for a formula.
After sorting, cost(M) is sum over i at least n over 2 (0-indexed) of max(0, M minus A i). Binary search the largest M in A n over 2 to A n over 2 plus k with cost(M) at most k; O of n log k.
clips.script: After sorting, cost(M) is sum over i at least n over 2 (0-indexed) of max(0, M minus eh i). Binary search the largest M in eh n over 2 to eh n over 2 plus k with cost(M) at most k; O of n log k.

clips.text: Sort A. The median is at least M iff every element from index n over 2 to the end is at least M, and the cheapest way there raises each such A i less than M up to M, costing the sum of max(0, M minus A i) over i at least n over 2. This cost grows with M, so binary search the largest M in A n over 2 to A n over 2 plus k whose cost is at most k. Use long long: M can reach 2 times 10 to the 9, and stopping the sum as soon as it passes k keeps it small. O of n log n plus n log k.
clips.script: Sort eh. The median is at least M iff every element from index n over 2 to the end is at least M, and the cheapest way there raises each such eh i less than M up to M, costing the sum of max(0, M minus eh i) over i at least n over 2. This cost grows with M, so binary search the largest M in eh n over 2 to eh n over 2 plus k whose cost is at most k. Use long long: M can reach 2 times 10 to the 9, and stopping the sum as soon as it passes k keeps it small. O of n log n plus n log k.

clips.text: If Apollinaria can bake c cookies, can she bake c minus 1? How much magic powder does a fixed number of cookies need?
Baking is monotone in the number of cookies, and checking a fixed count c is a single sum, so binary search on c: the answer is the largest c whose powder requirement is at most k.

need(c) is sum over i of max(0, A i times c minus b i). Search c in 0 to 2 times 10 to the 9 (b i plus k at most 2 times 10 to the 9 and A i at least 1). A i times c reaches 2 times 10 to the 18, which still fits in long long, but break out of the sum as soon as it exceeds k.
clips.script: need(c) is sum over i of max(0, eh i times c minus b i). Search c in 0 to 2 times 10 to the 9 (b i plus k at most 2 times 10 to the 9 and eh i at least 1). eh i times c reaches 2 times 10 to the 18, which still fits in long long, but break out of the sum as soon as it exceeds k.

clips.text: For c cookies ingredient i needs A i times c grams, so the powder required is the sum of max(0, A i times c minus b i), which never decreases as c grows. Binary search the largest c with requirement at most k, keeping lo is 0 feasible and hi is 2 times 10 to the 9 plus 1 infeasible; each check is O of n, so the total is O of n log 2 times 10 to the 9. The usual WA is overflow: A i times c is up to 2 times 10 to the 18, and the running sum overflows if you keep adding after it passes k, so stop early.

clips.text: Fix a time T. Where can friend i be after T seconds, and what must be true of all these sets for everyone to meet?
Friend i can reach exactly the interval x i minus v i times T to x i plus v i times T, and every interval grows with T. So "can they meet within T" is monotone: binary search on the real number T.
Check: max(x i minus v i times T) at most min(x i plus v i times T). Search T in 0 to 10 to the 9 with 100 halvings rather than an epsilon loop; O of 100 times n.

Within time T friend i can stand anywhere in x i minus v i times T to x i plus v i times T, so all of them can meet iff the largest left end is at most the smallest right end. This only gets easier as T grows, so binary search T over 0 to 10 to the 9 (distance at most 10 to the 9, speed at least 1) for 100 iterations and print hi with 12 decimals. The fixed iteration count avoids an endless loop when hi minus lo stops shrinking in floating point. Ternary search on the meeting point also works, since the time to gather at p is max i the size of x i minus p over v i, a convex function of p.

Write the gathering time as a function of the meeting point x0. What does each person's term t i plus the size of x i minus x0 look like as a graph, and what happens when you take the maximum of several of them?
Each term is a V shape, so their maximum is convex in x0: it falls with slope minus 1, then rises with slope +1, with a single lowest point. That is exactly what ternary search on reals needs.
Ternary search x0 over 0 to 10 to the 8 for about 100 iterations; each evaluation is an O of n maximum. Print the final midpoint.

f(x0) is max i (t i plus the size of x i minus x0) is a maximum of convex functions, so it is convex, and because every piece has slope ±1 its minimum is a single point. Ternary search on 0 to 10 to the 8: evaluate f at the two thirds, discard the side with the larger value, repeat 100 times, and print (lo plus hi) over 2. That is O of 100 times n per test, fine for sum of n at most 2 times 10 to the 5. As a check, the optimum is also (min(x i minus t i) plus max(x i plus t i)) over 2, because f(x0) is max(max(x i plus t i) minus x0, x0 minus min(x i minus t i)).
In the final arrays there is a value T with min(A) at least T at least max(b). If you fix T, what is the cheapest way to get there?
clips.script: In the final arrays there is a value T with min(eh) at least T at least max(b). If you fix T, what is the cheapest way to get there?

clips.text: For a fixed T the cost is sum of max(0, T minus A i) plus sum of max(0, b i minus T), a sum of convex functions of T and therefore convex. Minimising a convex function over the integers is a job for ternary search.
clips.script: For a fixed T the cost is sum of max(0, T minus eh i) plus sum of max(0, b i minus T), a sum of convex functions of T and therefore convex. Minimising a convex function over the integers is a job for ternary search.

clips.text: Binary search for the first T in 1 to 10 to the 9 with cost(T) at most cost(T plus 1), the integer form of ternary search; each cost evaluation is O of n plus m. Keep the cost in long long.

Any valid final state has a threshold T between max(b) and min(A), and for a fixed T the cheapest fix raises every A i below T to T and lowers every b i above T to T. That cost is a sum of convex piecewise-linear functions of T, so it is convex, and the first T with cost(T) at most cost(T plus 1) is a minimiser. Binary search that T in 1 to 10 to the 9: about 30 rounds of two O of n plus m evaluations. The cost can reach 10 to the 5 times 10 to the 9, so use long long.
clips.script: Any valid final state has a threshold T between max(b) and min(eh), and for a fixed T the cheapest fix raises every eh i below T to T and lowers every b i above T to T. That cost is a sum of convex piecewise-linear functions of T, so it is convex, and the first T with cost(T) at most cost(T plus 1) is a minimiser. Binary search that T in 1 to 10 to the 9: about 30 rounds of two O of n plus m evaluations. The cost can reach 10 to the 5 times 10 to the 9, so use long long.

clips.text: Work out the barrel temperature after an even number of cups, and after 2k plus 1 cups. Which of these can ever get close to a t above (h plus c) over 2?

Every even count gives exactly (h plus c) over 2, so if t at most (h plus c) over 2 the answer is 2. Otherwise only odd counts matter, and their temperature ((k plus 1)h plus kc) over (2k plus 1) decreases towards (h plus c) over 2 as k grows: monotone in k, so binary search on k.

Find the largest k with (k plus 1)h plus kc at least t(2k plus 1), then compare k and k plus 1 by cross-multiplying the two distances to t, all in long long, and print 2k plus 1 or 2k plus 3 (on a tie, the smaller).

If 2t at most h plus c, print 2. Otherwise binary search k in 0 to 10 to the 6 for the last k whose temperature T k is ((k plus 1)h plus kc) over (2k plus 1) is still at least t (k is 0 always qualifies because h at least t). The closest temperature is T k or T k plus 1: with d1 is (k plus 1)h plus kc minus t(2k plus 1) and d2 is t(2k plus 3) minus ((k plus 2)h plus (k plus 1)c), choose 2k plus 1 iff d1 times (2k plus 3) at most d2 times (2k plus 1). These products stay below about 10 to the 18, so the comparison is exact in long long; comparing doubles here is the usual WA on ties. Even counts never win, because T k plus 1 already lies strictly between (h plus c) over 2 and t.
The table has up to 2.5 times 10 to the 11 entries, far too many to list. But for a given number x, can you quickly count how many entries are at most x?

Row i holds i, 2i,..., m times i, so it has min(m, floor of x over i) entries at most x. That count grows with x, and the k-th smallest entry is the first x whose count reaches k: binary search on the value, not on a position.
Binary search x in 1 to n times m for the smallest x with sum of _i min(m, floor of x over i) at least k; O of n log(nm). Counts reach 2.5 times 10 to the 11, so use long long.

Let cnt(x) is sum of _i=1 to n min(m, floor of x over i), the number of table entries at most x; it never decreases as x grows. The answer is the smallest x with cnt(x) at least k, found by binary search over 1 to n times m in about 38 rounds of O of n. That smallest x always appears in the table: otherwise cnt(x minus 1) is cnt(x) and x minus 1 would qualify too. Keep x, k and the count in long long, since n times m reaches 2.5 times 10 to the 11.
For a fixed x, how do you compute the weakness in O of n? Then think about how it changes as x moves from very negative to very positive.

For fixed x the weakness is max(largest subarray sum, minus smallest subarray sum) of the sequence A i minus x: two Kadane passes. Each segment's the size of sum is convex in x and a maximum of convex functions is convex, so the weakness is unimodal in x: ternary search on a real x.
clips.script: For fixed x the weakness is max(largest subarray sum, minus smallest subarray sum) of the sequence eh i minus x: two Kadane passes. Each segment's the size of sum is convex in x and a maximum of convex functions is convex, so the weakness is unimodal in x: ternary search on a real x.

clips.text: Ternary search x over minus 10 to the 4 to 10 to the 4 for about 100 iterations, evaluating the weakness with Kadane each time: O of 100 times n. Print the weakness at the final x, not x itself.

Each segment sum sum of (A i minus x) is S minus len times x is linear in x, so its absolute value is convex, and the weakness, the maximum over all segments, is convex in x. Evaluate it in O of n as the larger of the maximum subarray sum and minus the minimum subarray sum of A i minus x (Kadane twice), and ternary search x in minus 10 to the 4 to 10 to the 4 for 100 iterations. The optimum lies in that range because for x below min(A) every term is positive and raising x lowers the total, and symmetrically above max(A). Use a fixed iteration count: 100 rounds of two O of n scans is 4 times 10 to the 7 steps, while a while (hi minus lo greater than eps) loop risks never ending.
clips.script: Each segment sum sum of (eh i minus x) is S minus len times x is linear in x, so its absolute value is convex, and the weakness, the maximum over all segments, is convex in x. Evaluate it in O of n as the larger of the maximum subarray sum and minus the minimum subarray sum of eh i minus x (Kadane twice), and ternary search x in minus 10 to the 4 to 10 to the 4 for 100 iterations. The optimum lies in that range because for x below min(eh) every term is positive and raising x lowers the total, and symmetrically above max(eh). Use a fixed iteration count: 100 rounds of two O of n scans is 4 times 10 to the 7 steps, while a while (hi minus lo greater than eps) loop risks never ending.

clips.text: Maria starts at the south-western point and heads north. Which way round the lake does that send her, and on which side of her is the water?

Starting north from the lowest, then westernmost, point means the track runs clockwise, so the lake is on her right. Ignoring a turn puts her in the water exactly when the turn is to the left, and the sign of a cross product of consecutive directions tells left from right.
For each vertex p i with 1 at most i at most n minus 1, compute cross(p i minus p i minus 1, p i plus 1 minus p i) and count the positive values (left turns). O of n, all in integers.

Because the first section goes north from the lowest, then westernmost, point, the track is traversed clockwise and the lake (the polygon's interior) is on the right. A turn is dangerous iff going straight on enters the interior, which happens exactly at the left turns of a clockwise walk. Count the vertices p 1 to p n minus 1 where cross(p i minus p i minus 1, p i plus 1 minus p i) greater than 0; the start vertex is a right turn and never counts. Since every section is axis-parallel, right turns minus left turns is 4, which gives the closed form (n minus 4) over 2 as a check.
Look at each line only where it meets the two borders x1 and x2. If two lines cross strictly inside the strip, what happens to their vertical order between x1 and x2?

Two lines cross strictly inside iff their order at x1 is the reverse of their order at x2. So sort the lines by height at x1 and look for a pair whose heights at x2 are out of order: a sweep across the strip that only needs its two ends.
Compute y1 is k times x1 plus b and y2 is k times x2 plus b in long long, sort the pairs (y1, y2) lexicographically, and answer YES iff some adjacent pair has y2 strictly decreasing. O of n log n.

Map every line to (y1, y2), its heights at x1 and x2, computed exactly in long long (up to about 10 to the 12). Lines i and j meet strictly inside the strip iff y1 i minus y1 j and y2 i minus y2 j have strictly opposite signs. After sorting by (y1, y2) such a pair exists iff the y2 sequence is not non-decreasing, which one scan of adjacent pairs decides. Breaking ties at x1 by y2 keeps lines that meet exactly on the left border from being reported, and testing for a strict decrease ignores lines that meet on the right border.
Every road is an infinite line. Can a route from home to the university avoid crossing a road that has home on one side and the university on the other?

Each road that separates the two points must be crossed at least once, and no other road ever needs crossing. So the answer is the number of separating lines, and "which side of the line" is the sign of A times x plus b times y plus c.
clips.script: Each road that separates the two points must be crossed at least once, and no other road ever needs crossing. So the answer is the number of separating lines, and "which side of the line" is the sign of eh times x plus b times y plus c.

clips.text: For each road compute s1 is A times x1 plus b times y1 plus c and s2 is A times x2 plus b times y2 plus c in long long and count the roads where the signs differ. Compare the signs directly: s1 times s2 can reach 4 times 10 to the 24 and overflow.
clips.script: For each road compute s1 is eh times x1 plus b times y1 plus c and s2 is eh times x2 plus b times y2 plus c in long long and count the roads where the signs differ. Compare the signs directly: s1 times s2 can reach 4 times 10 to the 24 and overflow.

clips.text: A road separates home and the university iff A times x plus b times y plus c has different signs at the two points, and every route between them must cross each such road, so the answer is at least that count. The straight segment from home to the university (shifted slightly if it passes through an intersection) crosses exactly those roads once each, so the count is achieved. The values reach about 2 times 10 to the 12, fine in long long, but compare (s1 greater than 0) with (s2 greater than 0) instead of multiplying them. O of n.
clips.script: A road separates home and the university iff eh times x plus b times y plus c has different signs at the two points, and every route between them must cross each such road, so the answer is at least that count. clips.text: What is the cheapest way to break convexity? Think about one vertex and its two neighbours only.

Convexity breaks once some vertex p i can reach the line through its neighbours. Its distance to that line is the size of cross(p i plus 1 minus p i minus 1, p i minus p i minus 1) divided by the size of p i plus 1 minus p i minus 1 (twice the triangle area over the base), and moving the vertex and its neighbours towards each other closes the gap at half the cost.

The answer is the minimum over all i of h i over 2, where h i is that distance, including the wrap-around triples. Compute the cross product exactly (_ int128, since differences reach 2 times 10 to the 9) and do only the final division in long double. O of n.

For each vertex let h i be the distance from p i to the line through p i minus 1 and p i plus 1, computed as the size of cross(p i plus 1 minus p i minus 1, p i minus p i minus 1) / the size of p i plus 1 minus p i minus 1. Moving p i by h i over 2 towards that line and both neighbours by h i over 2 towards p i makes the three points collinear, and no smaller D can do it, so the answer is min i h i over 2. The cross product is exact in _ int128 and the division is the only floating-point step. Remember the triples that wrap around the end of the vertex list.
Try small cases: for a triangle T is a hexagon, and for a square T is a square. What property must P have for T to look like P?

T is the set of all differences A minus B with A and B in P, so T is always centrally symmetric (if v is in T, so is minus v). P and T can only be similar if P is centrally symmetric too, and then T is just P scaled by 2. That is a check on vertex vectors, with no areas or angles.
clips.script: T is the set of all differences eh minus B with eh and B in P, so T is always centrally symmetric (if v is in T, so is minus v). P and T can only be similar if P is centrally symmetric too, and then T is just P scaled by 2. That is a check on vertex vectors, with no areas or angles.

clips.text: Answer NO if n is odd. Otherwise check that p i plus p i plus n over 2 is the same vector for every i less than n over 2 (twice the centre, so it stays in integers). O of n.

T is P plus ( minus P) is centrally symmetric for every P, and similarity preserves central symmetry, so P must be centrally symmetric; conversely, if it is, T is P scaled by 2 about its centre. For a convex polygon listed in order, central symmetry means n is even and each vertex p i and its opposite p i plus n over 2 have the same midpoint. Compare the sums p i plus p i plus n over 2 in long long instead of halving them, so no fractions appear. O of n.
With up to 10 to the 5 points you cannot try every pair of lines. If an answer exists, what can you say about the first three points?
Two lines cover three points only if two of those points share a line (pigeonhole). So one of the lines through (p0, p1), (p0, p2) or (p1, p2) belongs to any valid answer.

For each of the three candidate lines, set aside the points on it (cross product zero) and check that the rest are collinear, again with cross products. Coordinates reach 10 to the 9, so compute cross products in _ int128. O of n; with n at most 4 the answer is YES.

If n at most 4, answer YES. Otherwise two of p0, p1, p2 lie on the same line of any valid pair, so that line is one of the three lines through two of them. For each candidate, collect the points not on it and test whether they are all collinear with the first two leftovers; zero, one or two leftovers always pass. Every test is the sign of a cross product: coordinate differences reach 2 times 10 to the 9, so the products are near the long long limit and _ int128 removes any doubt. Three candidates of O of n each give O of n.
A rectangle is fixed by a bottom and a top horizontal segment plus two vertical segments that reach both. If you fix the bottom segment, what do you need to know about each vertical segment?

Fix the bottom h1 and keep only the verticals that cross it. For a top segment h2 above it, the usable verticals are those that still reach h2.y and whose x lies in the overlap of h1 and h2; c of them give c(c minus 1) over 2 rectangles. Sweeping h2 upwards, verticals only ever drop out, so this is a sweep line over y with a Fenwick tree over x.

Sort horizontals by y. For each h1: add the verticals crossing it to a Fenwick tree indexed by x and sort them by top end; walk h2 upwards, removing verticals whose top is below h2.y, then count the ones in max(x1) to min(x2) with a range query. O of n squared log C with C is 10 to the 4.

Split the segments into horizontal and vertical ones and sort the horizontals by y. For each bottom segment h1, take the verticals v with h1.x1 at most v x at most h1.x2 and v.y1 at most h1.y at most v.y2, add 1 at position v x in a Fenwick tree, and sort them by top end. Sweep the horizontals h2 above h1 in increasing y: first remove the verticals whose top is below h2.y, since they reach neither h2 nor anything higher, then let c be the number left with x in max(h1.x1 up to h2.x1, min(h1.x2, h2.x2) and add c(c minus 1) over 2. Empty the tree before the next h1. The total is O of n squared log C, and the answer can reach about 10 to the 13, so use long long.
The pair with the smallest angle must be neighbours in some ordering of the vectors. Which ordering?

Sort the vectors by polar angle; the minimum non-oriented angle is between two cyclically adjacent vectors, including the last and the first. The real difficulty is precision: two candidate angles can differ by less than double can resolve, so compare them in integers instead of with atan2.

Polar-sort exactly: by half-plane first (y greater than 0, or y is 0 and x greater than 0), then by cross product. The angle between neighbours u and v is the direction of the vector (dot(u, v), the size of cross(u, v)), which lies in the upper half-plane, so compare two such angles by the sign of their cross product. Everything fits in long long; O of n log n.

Sort the vectors by angle without floating point: the half-plane y greater than 0 ∪ y is 0, x greater than 0 comes first, and inside a half a goes before b iff cross(A, b) greater than 0. For each of the n cyclic neighbour pairs, the non-oriented angle is atan2(the size of cross, dot), so represent it by the point (dot, the size of cross), whose coordinates are at most 2 times 10 to the 8 in absolute value. Angle 1 is smaller than angle 2 iff cross((dot1, the size of cross1), (dot2, the size of cross2)) greater than 0, a value below 10 to the 17 and exact in long long. Keep the best pair and print its original indices. Plain double atan2 is known to fail on this problem; long double atan2l is the common workaround, but the integer comparison removes the question.

Angle 1 is smaller than angle 2 iff cross((dot1, the size of cross1), (dot2, the size of cross2)) greater than 0, a value below 10 to the 17 and exact in long long. clips.text: The path must enclose every cow, and a shortest closed path around a set of points follows the outermost ones. What does it cost to walk from one outer cow to the next when the shepherd can also step diagonally?

Only the convex hull of the cows matters. With diagonal steps, going from one hull vertex to the next takes max(the size of dx, the size of dy) moves (the Chebyshev distance), so the answer is the hull perimeter measured that way, plus a constant for keeping the cows strictly inside.

Build the hull with the monotone chain after removing duplicate cows, sum max(the size of dx, the size of dy) over its edges, and add 4. A single point gives 4, and for collinear cows the hull is a segment counted once in each direction.

Compute the convex hull of the cows with Andrew's monotone chain in O of n log n. Each hull edge from (x1, y1) to (x2, y2) costs max(the size of x2 minus x1, the size of y2 minus y1) moves with eight-direction steps, and keeping the herd strictly inside adds exactly 4 moves in total (check it on a single cow: the shortest loop around one point is 4 diagonal steps). So the answer is 4 plus the sum of the Chebyshev lengths of the hull edges, all in integers. Handle degenerate hulls: when all cows share a point the hull has no edges, and when they are collinear it is a segment walked there and back.
A is convex. If every vertex of B is strictly inside A, can any point of B still be outside?
clips.script: eh is convex. If every vertex of B is strictly inside eh, can any point of B still be outside?

clips.text: A convex region contains every segment between two of its points, so B is strictly inside A iff all m vertices of B are. That leaves m point-in-convex-polygon queries with n up to 10 to the 5, so each query needs O of log n: binary search over the fan of triangles from one vertex of A.
clips.script: A convex region contains every segment between two of its points, so B is strictly inside A iff all m vertices of B are. That leaves m point-in-convex-polygon queries with n up to 10 to the 5, so each query needs O of log n: binary search over the fan of triangles from one vertex of eh.

clips.text: Reverse A to counter-clockwise order. For a point q: reject unless q is strictly left of A0: that is, A1 and strictly right of A0: that is, A(n minus 1); binary search the last i with q left of or on the ray A0: that is, Ai; then q is strictly inside iff it is strictly left of the edge Ai: that is, A(i plus 1). Use _ int128 for the cross products.
clips.script: Reverse eh to counter-clockwise order. For a point q: reject unless q is strictly left of A0: that is, A1 and strictly right of A0: that is, A(n minus 1); binary search the last i with q left of or on the ray A0: that is, Ai; then q is strictly inside iff it is strictly left of the edge Ai: that is, A(i plus 1). Use _ int128 for the cross products.

clips.text: Since A is convex, B is strictly inside A iff every vertex of B is strictly inside A. Turn A counter-clockwise and fan it from A0: q is strictly inside iff cross(A1 minus A0, q minus A0) greater than 0, cross(A(n minus 1) minus A0, q minus A0) less than 0, and cross(A(i plus 1) minus Ai, q minus Ai) greater than 0 for the sector i found by binary search on the sign of cross(Ai minus A0, q minus A0). Each query is O of log n, so the total is O of n plus m log n. Points on an edge of A, including the first and last edges from A0, must give NO, which is why every test is strict; with coordinates up to 10 to the 9 the cross products are computed in _ int128.
clips.script: Since eh is convex, B is strictly inside A iff every vertex of B is strictly inside eh. Turn A counter-clockwise and fan it from A0: q is strictly inside iff cross(A1 minus A0, q minus A0) greater than 0, cross(A(n minus 1) minus A0, q minus A0) less than 0, and cross(A(i plus 1) minus Ai, q minus Ai) greater than 0 for the sector i found by binary search on the sign of cross(Ai minus A0, q minus A0). Each query is O of log n, so the total is O of n plus m log n. Points on an edge of eh, including the first and last edges from A0, must give NO, which is why every test is strict; with coordinates up to 10 to the 9 the cross products are computed in _ int128.

clips.text: In the final sequence the tanks fall into blocks, each set to its own average. How should the first block be chosen to make the first value as small as possible?

The first value is minimised by the prefix with the smallest average, and then the same rule repeats on the rest. Draw the prefix sums as points (i, S i): a block's average is the slope between two of these points, so the optimal blocks are exactly the edges of the lower convex hull.

Build that hull with a stack of blocks (sum, length): push each tank as its own block and, while the block below has an average at least the top block's, merge them. Compare averages by cross-multiplying in long long and print each block's average to 9 decimals. O of n.

Treat the prefix sums as points P i is (i, S i). Making the first value small means choosing the prefix with the smallest slope from P 0, which is the first edge of the lower convex hull of these points; the later blocks follow the later hull edges, with increasing slopes. A stack does this in O of n: each tank starts a block (A i, 1), and while the block below has average at least the top one (sum below times len top at least sum top times len below, exact in long long since sums at most 10 to the 12 and lengths at most 10 to the 6), merge them. Print sum / len once per tank in the block. With n is 10 to the 6, read integers rather than doubles and buffer the output.
clips.script: Treat the prefix sums as points P i is (i, S i). Making the first value small means choosing the prefix with the smallest slope from P 0, which is the first edge of the lower convex hull of these points; the later blocks follow the later hull edges, with increasing slopes. A stack does this in O of n: each tank starts a block (eh i, 1), and while the block below has average at least the top one (sum below times len top at least sum top times len below, exact in long long since sums at most 10 to the 12 and lengths at most 10 to the 6), merge them. Print sum / len once per tank in the block. With n is 10 to the 6, read integers rather than doubles and buffer the output.

clips.text: Once tree i is cut completely, every later charge costs b i or less, and once tree n is cut, charging is free. Which trees are worth cutting completely, and in what order?

Cut a chain of trees completely in increasing index order, ending at tree n; every other tree is finished afterwards for free. Moving from tree j to tree i costs A i charges at b j each, so dp of i is min j less than i dp of j plus b j times A i. Each j is a line with slope b j evaluated at x is A i: a lower-envelope query.
clips.script: Cut a chain of trees completely in increasing index order, ending at tree n; every other tree is finished afterwards for free. Moving from tree j to tree i costs eh i charges at b j each, so dp of i is min j less than i dp of j plus b j times eh i. Each j is a line with slope b j evaluated at x is eh i: a lower-envelope query.

clips.text: Slopes b j arrive in decreasing order and the query points A i in increasing order, so the monotone convex hull trick with a deque gives O of n. dp values reach 10 to the 18, so do the useless-line test in _ int128. The answer is dp of n.

clips.text: Let dp of i be the minimum cost until tree i is cut completely; dp of 1 is 0 because A 1 is 1 uses the initial charge. If j was the last tree cut completely before i, cutting tree i costs A i charges at b j each, so dp of i is min j less than i (dp of j plus b j times A i), and after tree n every charge is free, so the answer is dp of n. Each j is the line y is b j times x plus dp of j; slopes decrease and query points increase, so a deque-based convex hull trick answers all queries in O of n total. Compare intersection points by cross-multiplying in _ int128, because intercepts reach 10 to the 18 and slopes 10 to the 9.

clips.text: No rectangle contains another, so sorting by x also sorts y in the opposite order. For a chosen set in that order, what does the union look like, and how much area does each new rectangle add?

With x increasing and y decreasing the union is a staircase: adding rectangle i after j adds (x i minus x j) times y i. So dp of i is x i times y i minus A i plus max(0, max j less than i dp of j minus x j times y i), and the inner maximum is over lines with slope minus x j evaluated at y i: the convex hull trick.

So dp of i is x i times y i minus eh i plus max(0, max j less than i dp of j minus x j times y i), and the inner maximum is over lines with slope minus x j evaluated at y i: the convex hull trick.

clips.text: Slopes minus x j decrease as j grows and the query points y i decrease, so a monotone deque works in O of n after sorting (substitute z is minus y if you want the min-with-increasing-queries form). Read the 10 to the 6 lines fast, use _ int128 in the line test, and take the best dp of i overall.

Sort by x ascending; since no rectangle is nested, y is then strictly descending. Rectangle i placed after j adds the strip (x i minus x j) times y i to the union, so dp of i is x i times y i minus A i plus max(0, max j less than i(dp of j minus x j times y i)), and the answer is the largest dp of i. Each j contributes the line y ↦ dp of j minus x j times y; the slopes decrease and the queries y i decrease, so keep the upper envelope in a deque and drop lines from the front as queries advance (or negate, z is minus y, and reuse a min-hull with increasing queries), O of n after an O of n log n sort. Values reach 10 to the 18, so the intersection comparison needs _ int128, and 3 times 10 to the 6 input numbers need fast reading.
