clips.text: Splitting a day between projects gives a daily rate that is a weighted average of the projects' vectors (A i, b i). Which daily rates can Mikhail achieve?
clips.script: Splitting a day between projects gives a daily rate that is a weighted average of the projects' vectors (eh i, b i). Which daily rates can Mikhail achieve?

clips.text: The achievable daily rates are the convex hull of the points (A i, b i). Because he needs only at least p and q, the dominated corners (max A, 0), (0, max b) and (0, 0) can be added. In T days he collects T times rate, so the best rate is the hull point furthest along the ray from the origin towards (p, q).
clips.script: The achievable daily rates are the convex hull of the points (eh i, b i). Because he needs only at least p and q, the dominated corners (max eh, 0), (0, max b) and (0, 0) can be added. In T days he collects T times rate, so the best rate is the hull point furthest along the ray from the origin towards (p, q).

clips.text: Build the hull of all points plus the three corners. For each hull edge u: that is, v whose endpoints are not both strictly on the same side of the line through the origin and (p, q), intersect: t is cross(u, v) / cross((p, q), v minus u). The largest t is where the ray leaves the hull, and the answer is 1 over t. O of n log n.

Working on project i for a fraction of each day gives a convex combination of the vectors (A i, b i), so in T days Mikhail can collect exactly T times any point of their convex hull. Only "at least p and q" matters, so adding (max A, 0), (0, max b) and the origin changes nothing and turns the region into everything the projects dominate. The best rate is t times (p, q) with the largest t inside this hull, found by intersecting the ray from the origin through (p, q) with every hull edge it can cross; then T is 1 over t. Hull building and the side tests are exact in long long (coordinates at most 10 to the 6); only the final t and 1 over t are floating point.

clips.text: Every parabola here has the same x squared term. What happens to a parabola, and to "strictly above it", if you subtract x squared from every y?

Map each point (x, y) to (x, y minus x squared). The parabola y is x squared plus bx plus c becomes the straight line Y, which is bx plus c, and a point is strictly above the parabola iff its image is strictly above the line. So you are counting lines through two points with no point strictly above them: the edges of the upper convex hull.

For each x keep only the highest transformed point, sort by x, and build the upper hull with a monotone stack, popping when the turn is not strictly clockwise so that collinear points merge into one edge. The answer is the number of hull points minus 1. Y reaches about 10 to the 12, so use _ int128 for cross products.

Subtracting x squared maps each U-shaped parabola through two points with different x to the line through their images, and keeps "strictly above" intact. A line through two transformed points has no point strictly above it iff it supports the upper convex hull, so the answer is the number of distinct lines along the upper hull. Keep only the largest Y for each x (a lower point with the same x can never lie on such a line), sort by x, and build the upper chain, popping while the cross product is at least 0 so that collinear points merge and each line is counted once. The answer is the hull size minus 1, in O of n log n, with cross products in _ int128 because the transformed coordinates reach about 10 to the 12.
Add the tens, then the ones
Start from the bigger number and add the other one place by place, biggest place first. Each step is a single-digit addition, and the answer comes out in the order you type it.
When to use it: No column adds up to 10 or more, like 43 plus 25.
43 plus 25
43 plus 20 is 63
63 plus 5 is 68
No column reaches 10, so each digit of the answer is just the two digits added.
Settle the carry first, right to left

Before you type anything, add the ones digits. If they make 10 or more, you know the last digit of the answer and that the next column goes up by one. Work leftwards the same way, then type the whole answer left to right without hesitating.
When to use it: A column adds up to 10 or more, like 47 plus 38 or 69 plus 56. Shortcut: if one number ends in 8 or 9, round it up and take the difference back off (47 plus 39 is 47 plus 40 minus 1).
47 plus 38
ones: 7 plus 8 is 15, write 5, carry 1
tens: 4 plus 3 plus 1 is 8
answer: 85
Right to left: a column that makes 10 or more writes its last digit and carries 1 (red) into the next column.
Take away the biggest place first
Subtract the second number place by place, biggest place first. No digit ever goes below zero, so each step is a single fact.
When to use it: Every digit on top is at least the digit underneath, like 87 minus 25.
87 minus 25
87 minus 20 is 67
67 minus 5 is 62
Hop back by each place of the number you take away, biggest first.
Round the number you take away

Borrowing digit by digit means holding a change in your head while you work. Instead, round the number you are subtracting up to the next ten, subtract that, and add back the extra. Both steps are clean.
When to use it: A digit on top is smaller than the one underneath, like 84 minus 29 or 72 minus 36. It is quickest when the number you take away ends in 7, 8 or 9.
84 minus 29
round 29 up to 30 (that's 1 too many)
84 minus 30 is 54
54 plus 1 is 55
Hop back a round 30, then forward the 1 you over-did.
Bridge through the hundred

Split the top number into its hundreds and the rest. Take the second number away from the hundreds, then add the rest back on. For 100 minus 56, the digits pair up: tens make 9 (5 and 4), ones make 10 (6 and 4), so it is 44.
When to use it: The answer drops below a hundred boundary, like 134 minus 56 (below 100) or 523 minus 48 (below 500).
134 minus 56
134 is 100 plus 34
100 minus 56 is 44
44 plus 34 is 78
The gap from 56 up to 134 is 44 to reach 100, plus 34 more: 78.
Know the facts cold

Times-table facts should be recall, not calculation. Until a fact is automatic, rebuild it from an anchor you do know: times 5 is half of times 10, times 9 is times 10 minus one lot, times 4 and times 8 are repeated doubling, and times 12 is times 10 plus times 2. Every time you rebuild a fact, it sticks a little more.
When to use it: Both numbers are 12 or below once you ignore trailing zeros (7 times 60 is 7 times 6 with a zero on the end).
7 times 8
double 7 three times: 14, 28, 56
7 rows of 8 is 56. Split at 5 (green) when 5 is your anchor.
Split the big number by place value
Multiply the biggest place first, then the next, then add. Going left to right means you hold one running total while you work out small products, and the answer builds in the order you type it.
When to use it: A single digit times a bigger number, like 7 times 64. Most of a default Zetamac round is this kind of question.
7 times 64
7 times 60 is 420
7 times 4 is 28
420 plus 28 is 448
Split 64 into 60 plus 4. The answer is the total area, 448.
Times ten, plus a bit
11 times n is 10 times n plus one more n. 12 times n is 10 times n plus double n. Putting a zero on the end is free, so the only real work is one addition.
When to use it: An 11 or 12 times a bigger number, like 11 times 47 or 12 times 38.
12 times 47
47 times 10 is 470
47 times 2 is 94
470 plus 94 is 564
12 is 10 plus 2: 47 times 10 plus 47 times 2 is 564.
Split the smaller number, multiply twice

Break the smaller number into tens and ones, multiply the other number by each, and add. 23 times 47 is 20 times 47 plus 3 times 47. If both numbers sit close to a round number, (A minus d)(A plus d) is a squared minus d squared is faster still.
clips.script: Break the smaller number into tens and ones, multiply the other number by each, and add. 23 times 47 is 20 times 47 plus 3 times 47. If both numbers sit close to a round number, (eh minus d)(eh plus d) is a squared minus d squared is faster still.

clips.text: When to use it: Both numbers are 13 or more, like 23 times 47. This only appears when you widen the multiplication ranges.
23 times 47
20 times 47 is 940
3 times 47 is 141
Split 47 into 40 plus 7 and 23 into 20 plus 3. The answer is the total area, 1081.
Ask the multiplication question
Don't divide. Ask "what times the divisor gives this?" and answer with a times-table fact you already know. If the number ends in zeros, drop them, find the fact, and put them back.
When to use it: The answer is 12 or less once you ignore trailing zeros, like 56 divided by 7 or 420 divided by 7.
56 divided by 7
7 times? is 56
7 times 8 is 56, so 8
56 is an area 7 tall. Fill it with the widest round chunks that fit; the widths add up to the answer, 8.
Take out the biggest chunk first
Find the largest round multiple that fits: 7 times 60 is 420 fits inside 448. Take it away, and divide what is left with a single fact (28 divided by 7 is 4). The answer is the chunks added up: 64.
When to use it: Dividing by a single digit when the answer is above 12, like 448 divided by 7.
448 divided by 7
448 minus 420 is 28 left
28 divided by 7 is 4
60 plus 4 is 64
448 is an area 7 tall. Fill it with the widest round chunks that fit; the widths add up to the answer, 64.
Chunk by tens of 11 or 12
Same method as other chunked divisions, but the chunks are 110, 220, 330… for 11 and 120, 240, 360… for 12. Find the biggest chunk that fits, then divide the remainder with a single fact.
When to use it: Dividing by 11 or 12 when the answer is above 12, like 564 divided by 12.
564 divided by 12
12 times 40 is 480
564 minus 480 is 84 left
84 divided by 12 is 7
40 plus 7 is 47
564 is an area 12 tall. Fill it with the widest round chunks that fit; the widths add up to the answer, 47.
Estimate the tens, then fix the ones
Round the divisor to estimate the tens of the answer: 1081 divided by 23 is a bit under 1081 divided by 20 about 54, so try 40. 23 times 40 is 920 leaves 161, and 23 times 7 is 161. The answer is 47.
When to use it: The divisor is 13 or more, like 1081 divided by 23. This only appears when you widen the multiplication ranges.
1081 divided by 23
23 times 40 is 920
1081 minus 920 is 161 left
161 divided by 23 is 7
1081 is an area 23 tall. Fill it with the widest round chunks that fit; the widths add up to the answer, 47.
Line up the points, then work in whole numbers

Give both numbers the same number of decimal places and treat them as whole tenths or hundredths: 4.7 plus 0.38 is 470 plus 38 is 508 hundredths, so 5.08. Then put the point back. Adding digits from different places is the only real mistake, and this makes it impossible.
When to use it: An addition or subtraction where at least one number has a decimal point, like 4.7 plus 0.38 or 7.25 minus 0.6.
in hundredths: 470 plus 38 is 508
put the point back: 5.08
Line the points up and pad with zeros so every number has the same number of decimal places.
Multiply whole numbers, then place the point

Ignore the decimal points and multiply the whole numbers with your usual method. Count the decimal places in the question and give the answer that many: 0.7 times 64, then 7 times 64 is 448, then one place: that is, 44.8. A quick size check catches slips: 0.7 of 64 must be a bit less than 64.
When to use it: A multiplication where either number has a decimal point, like 0.7 times 64 or 1.2 times 3.5.
0.7 times 64
ignore the points: 7 times 64 is 448
one decimal place in the question: 44.8
Multiply the whole numbers, then give the answer as many decimal places as the question had.
Make the divisor whole first

Moving the decimal point the same number of places in both numbers doesn't change the answer, so move it until the divisor is whole: 44.8 divided by 0.7 becomes 448 divided by 7 is 64. If the number you're dividing still has a point, work in tenths or hundredths and put the point back at the end.
When to use it: A division where either number has a decimal point, like 44.8 divided by 0.7 or 4.48 divided by 7.
44.8 divided by 0.7
move both points one place right: 448 divided by 7
448 divided by 7 is 64
Moving both points the same way leaves the answer unchanged; make the divisor whole first.
Fire that starts on every edge and moves inwards at speed v reaches a point after (its distance to the boundary) over v. So which point of the forest burns last?

The last point is the centre of the largest circle that fits inside the polygon, and the time is its radius R divided by v. The polygon may be non-convex, so binary-search on R instead: is there a point inside the forest that stays at least R away from every edge?

For a fixed R each edge rules out a "pill": every point within R of that edge (a strip plus a disk at each end). If an allowed point survives, so does a corner of the allowed region, and every corner is an intersection of two pill boundaries (line–line, line–circle or circle–circle), so test those points for being inside the polygon and at distance at least R from all edges.

The answer is the largest inscribed circle: print R over v and its centre. Binary-search R; for each R generate the pairwise intersections of the edges shifted by R and the radius-R circles around the vertices, and accept R if some candidate lies inside the polygon at distance at least R minus ε from every edge, remembering that point as the answer. Shift each edge to both sides so the winding order does not matter; the inside-polygon test discards the wrong ones. Checking candidates against the edges with an early exit keeps each step fast, and about 50 iterations reach 10 to the -6.
A wall can fail in two ways: a gap or an overlap. If you already knew there were no overlaps, what single number would tell you there are no gaps?

Bricks that do not overlap and whose areas add up to the area of their bounding box must cover it exactly. So the real work is detecting an overlap among 10 to the 6 rectangles, which is a sweep-line job: sweep along x and keep the y-intervals of the active bricks sorted.

Compare the summed areas with the bounding box using 128-bit integers (the sum can reach 10 to the 22). Then sort start and end events by x, process ends before starts at the same x, and keep active y up to y plus h intervals in an ordered set; a new interval can only overlap its predecessor or successor, so check just those two. O of n log n.

The bricks form a wall iff (1) their areas sum to the area of their bounding box and (2) no two bricks share interior points. Check (1) in 128-bit arithmetic. For (2) sweep over x: at each x first remove the bricks that end there, then insert those that start, and reject if a new y-interval overlaps a neighbour in the ordered set (sharing an edge is fine). Together the two conditions mean every point of the box is covered exactly once. O of n log n, with fast input for a million lines.

The checker only counts holes in each 4-connected blob, so you can draw C1 as crude blobs. The awkward part is that the word C2 must also sit somewhere in the picture, and every letter you write belongs to some blob.

Build it constructively: one blob per letter of C1 with 0, 1 or 2 holes (B has 2; A, D, O, P, Q, R have 1), with a column of dots between blobs. Fill the blobs with a letter that occurs in no colour name, such as X, so no row can spell a colour by accident, and make one full row of one blob read exactly C2.
clips.script: Build it constructively: one blob per letter of C1 with 0, 1 or 2 holes (B has 2; eh, D, O, P, Q, R have 1), with a column of dots between blobs. Fill the blobs with a letter that occurs in no colour name, such as X, so no row can spell a colour by accident, and make one full row of one blob read exactly C2.

clips.text: Make every blob 5 rows high: a solid block for 0 holes, a ring around a run of dots for 1 hole, and two such rings stacked (like XXX / X.X / XXX / X.X / XXX) for 2 holes. Make the first blob as wide as C2 and write C2 as its bottom row; it is attached to the blob, bounded by dots or the picture edge, and the picture stays far below 10 times 100.

Any picture that meets the rules is accepted, so build a simple one. Draw one 5-row blob per letter of C1, separated by a dot column: solid for 0 holes, a ring around one dot run for 1 hole, two stacked rings for 2 holes. Fill blobs with X, which appears in no colour name, and make the first blob exactly as wide as C2 with C2 as its bottom row, so C2 appears once as a whole word and no other colour can appear. The result is 5 rows by at most about 30 columns.

Stages run strictly in order and extra material can always be thrown away, so more material entering a stage is never worse. That leaves one question per stage: from x units of input, what is the most output you can end with?

Machines can be run any number of times, so a stage is an unbounded knapsack over the input you spend. The twist is the shared warehouse: after every run, the input left plus the output held must fit in k, and you may discard either material at any moment.

Let g of a be the most output you can hold with a units of input left. Start with g of x is 0 and go from A is x down to 0: g of A at least g of A plus 1 (discard one input), and each machine with MI at most A and A minus MI plus MO at most k gives g of A minus MI at least min(g of A plus MO, k minus (A minus MI)) (discard output first so the run fits). The stage passes g of 0 to the next one.
clips.script: Let g of a be the most output you can hold with a units of input left. Start with g of x is 0 and go from eh is x down to 0: g of eh at least g of eh plus 1 (discard one input), and each machine with MI at most eh and eh minus MI plus MO at most k gives g of eh minus MI at least min(g of eh plus MO, k minus (eh minus MI)) (discard output first so the run fits). The stage passes g of 0 to the next one.

clips.text: Process stages in order, carrying only the largest amount of the current material. Within a stage, g of a (best output with a units of input left) is filled from A is x down to 0 as an unbounded knapsack: discarding input gives g of A at least g of A plus 1, and running a machine needs A minus MI plus MO at most k and leaves min(g of A plus MO, k minus (A minus MI)) output, because overflowing output must be discarded before the run. That is O of k per machine, O of k times m overall. Sample 5 (s is k, so 7, one machine 3, then 5) shows why the room check matters: you must drop two units of ore first and end with 5, not 6.

Within a stage, g of a (best output with a units of input left) is filled from eh is x down to 0 as an unbounded knapsack: discarding input gives g of eh at least g of eh plus 1, and running a machine needs eh minus MI plus MO at most k and leaves min(g of eh plus MO, k minus (eh minus MI)) output, because overflowing output must be discarded before the run. That is O of k per machine, O of k times m overall. Sample 5 (s is k, so 7, one machine 3, then 5) shows why the room check matters: you must drop two units of ore first and end with 5, not 6.

clips.text: Fix the number of markers n first. How much walking time is left, and which n-gon with that perimeter encloses the most land?

With n markers the perimeter is P is t minus n times m, and among n-gons with a fixed perimeter the regular one has the largest area, P squared over (4n times tan(π/n)). Only n is left to choose; the area first rises and then falls as n grows, so ternary-search it.

If 3m at least t the answer is 0. Otherwise ternary-search the integer n in 3 to floor of (t minus 1) over m on f(n) is (t minus n times m) squared over (4n times tan(π/n)) until a few values remain, and check those directly. O of log(t over m) per case; doubles meet the 10 to the -6 relative error.

The optimal claim is convex (flip any dent outwards) and regular (moving a vertex to equalise its two edges increases area at a fixed perimeter), so with n markers the area is (t minus n times m) squared over (4n times tan(π/n)). Maximise over integers n at least 3 with n times m less than t by ternary search, finishing with a short linear scan; print 0 when no triangle is possible (3m at least t). Each case costs O of log(t over m), and the answers can reach about 10 to the 16, so compare with relative error in mind.
Suppose you knew the lowest height the walk may touch. Which hills and trails are then allowed, and how would you find the lowest possible highest point?

For a fixed minimum lo, only trails with both ends at least lo are usable; give each the weight max(h A, h b). The best walk then minimises its largest weight, a bottleneck path, and Kruskal's order finds it: add trails by increasing weight with a DSU until hills 1 and 2 are joined.
clips.script: For a fixed minimum lo, only trails with both ends at least lo are usable; give each the weight max(h eh, h b). The best walk then minimises its largest weight, a bottleneck path, and Kruskal's order finds it: add trails by increasing weight with a DSU until hills 1 and 2 are joined.

clips.text: Sort the trails by max(h A, h b) once. For every distinct height lo at most min(h 1, h 2), reset the DSU and add the trails with min(h A, h b) at least lo in sorted order until find(1) is find(2); the candidate is that trail's weight minus lo. Take the best candidate: O of n times m times α about 1.25 times 10 to the 8 cheap steps.
clips.script: Sort the trails by max(h eh, h b) once. For every distinct height lo at most min(h 1, h 2), reset the DSU and add the trails with min(h eh, h b) at least lo in sorted order until find(1) is find(2); the candidate is that trail's weight minus lo. Take the best candidate: O of n times m times α about 1.25 times 10 to the 8 cheap steps.

clips.text: Enumerate the minimum height lo among the hill heights (it can only be at most min(h 1, h 2)). With edges sorted by max endpoint height, run Kruskal from scratch, skipping edges with an endpoint below lo, and stop as soon as hills 1 and 2 are connected; the last added weight is the smallest possible maximum for this lo. The answer is the minimum of max minus lo over all lo. This is O of n times m times α(n) and fits in the 3.5 s limit.
Since A at least b, Charlie should always work while fresh. The only real decision is how many breaks to take, not when.
clips.script: Since eh at least b, Charlie should always work while fresh. The only real decision is how many breaks to take, not when.

clips.text: With k breaks there are W is n minus k times y working days split into k plus 1 runs, each with up to x fresh days, so the total is A times min(W, (k plus 1) times x) plus b times (the rest). This is linear in k while every run gets its full x fresh days and decreasing once all working days are fresh, so only the boundary values of k can win.
clips.script: With k breaks there are W is n minus k times y working days split into k plus 1 runs, each with up to x fresh days, so the total is eh times min(W, (k plus 1) times x) plus b times (the rest). This is linear in k while every run gets its full x fresh days and decreasing once all working days are fresh, so only the boundary values of k can win.

clips.text: Evaluate k is 0, k star is max(0, floor of (n minus x) over (x plus y)) (the most breaks that still leave full fresh runs) and k star plus 1, skipping any k with k times y greater than n, and print the best. Use 64-bit integers: the totals reach 10 to the 18.

Breaks only matter through their count k: the score is A times F plus b times (W minus F) with W is n minus k times y and F is min(W, (k plus 1) times x). For k up to k star is floor of (n minus x) over (x plus y) the score is linear in k (each extra break trades y times b of tired work for x times (A minus b) of extra freshness, the jury's x times a versus (x plus y) times b comparison), and beyond it the score A times W only falls. So the maximum is among k is 0, k star and k star plus 1. O of 1 per test with 64-bit integers.
clips.script: Breaks only matter through their count k: the score is eh times F plus b times (W minus F) with W is n minus k times y and F is min(W, (k plus 1) times x). For k up to k star is floor of (n minus x) over (x plus y) the score is linear in k (each extra break trades y times b of tired work for x times (eh minus b) of extra freshness, the jury's x times a versus (x plus y) times b comparison), and beyond it the score eh times W only falls. So the maximum is among k is 0, k star and k star plus 1. O of 1 per test with 64-bit integers.

clips.text: After switching at node z the search only visits z's subtree, so z must be an ancestor of K (or K itself). For each such ancestor, can you read K's position off one plain DFS and one plain BFS from the root?

Use DFS preorder positions: a DFS started at a visits A's subtree in exactly the global preorder order, and a BFS restricted to A's subtree visits each depth level in that same preorder order. So both hybrid positions become counts over a subtree and a depth.
clips.script: Use DFS preorder positions: a DFS started at a visits eh's subtree in exactly the global preorder order, and a BFS restricted to eh's subtree visits each depth level in that same preorder order. So both hybrid positions become counts over a subtree and a depth.

clips.text: BFS: that is, DFS: switching at a puts K at bfs of A plus dfs of K minus dfs of A; minimise over ancestors. DFS: that is, BFS: K lands at dfs of A minus 1 plus (nodes of A's subtree shallower than K) plus (nodes on K's level inside A's subtree with preorder at most dfs of K); get the first count from a subtree sum and the second by binary search on the sorted preorder numbers of K's level within tin of A to tout of A.
clips.script: BFS: that is, DFS: switching at a puts K at bfs of eh plus dfs of K minus dfs of eh; minimise over ancestors. DFS: that is, BFS: K lands at dfs of eh minus 1 plus (nodes of eh's subtree shallower than K) plus (nodes on K's level inside eh's subtree with preorder at most dfs of K); get the first count from a subtree sum and the second by binary search on the sorted preorder numbers of K's level within tin of eh to tout of eh.

clips.text: Root the tree at 1 with children in input order and compute 1-based positions bfs of and dfs of, subtree ranges tin to tout, and depths. Only ancestors of K are useful switch points. BFS: that is, DFS gives dfs of K plus min over ancestors A of (bfs of A minus dfs of A), as in the jury slides. DFS: that is, BFS at a gives dfs of A minus 1 plus the number of subtree nodes shallower than K plus the number of K-level subtree nodes up to K in preorder; with a subtree sum and binary search this is O of N log N, and the jury also shows an O of N walk up the ancestor chain.
clips.script: Root the tree at 1 with children in input order and compute 1-based positions bfs of and dfs of, subtree ranges tin to tout, and depths. Only ancestors of K are useful switch points. BFS: that is, DFS gives dfs of K plus min over ancestors eh of (bfs of eh minus dfs of eh), as in the jury slides. DFS: that is, BFS at a gives dfs of eh minus 1 plus the number of subtree nodes shallower than K plus the number of K-level subtree nodes up to K in preorder; with a subtree sum and binary search this is O of N log N, and the jury also shows an O of N walk up the ancestor chain.

clips.text: Only seven answers are possible: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 or 64 bits.
A b-bit word stores 0 … 2 to the b minus 1, so you want the smallest of those b with n less than 2 to the b. Since n at most 10 to the 18 less than 2 to the 60, 64 bits always suffice.

Try b is 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 in order and stop at the first with n less than 2 to the b, computing 2 to the b in 64-bit (never shift by 64); otherwise answer 64. Print "1 bit" for b is 1 and "b bits" otherwise.

Loop over b in 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and print the first b with n at most 2 to the b minus 1, else 64. Use 64-bit integers and do not compute 2 to the 64, which overflows. Only n is 1 gives the singular "1 bit".
If A less than m and m less than b, then every a must come before every b even if the word has no m. Which letters' relations do you actually need, and when is the word impossible?
clips.script: If eh less than m and m less than b, then every a must come before every b even if the word has no m. Which letters' relations do you actually need, and when is the word impossible?

clips.text: Take the transitive closure of the 26-letter "comes before" relation with Floyd–Warshall. The word is impossible exactly when two letters in it (possibly the same letter) are each before the other; otherwise the closure restricted to the word's letters is a DAG, and any topological order of it works.

Set before of A, b from the rules (A greater than b means b before A), then before of i, j or-equals before of i, m and before of m, j for all m, i, j. If some letters u, v of the word (u is v allowed) have before of u, v and before of v, u, print IMPOSSIBLE; otherwise topologically sort the word's letters and print each one as many times as it occurs.
clips.script: Set before of eh, b from the rules (eh greater than b means b before eh), then before of i, j or-equals before of i, m and before of m, j for all m, i, j. If some letters u, v of the word (u is v allowed) have before of u, v and before of v, u, print IMPOSSIBLE; otherwise topologically sort the word's letters and print each one as many times as it occurs.

clips.text: Build a 26 times 26 relation from the rules, close it with Floyd–Warshall (26 cubed steps), and check every pair of letters present in the word, including a letter with itself, for a cycle; cycles among letters that do not occur are harmless. If there is none, a topological sort of the present letters under the closure (or sorting them by the number of present letters before each) gives an order, and printing each letter cnt times is a valid answer. O of 26 cubed plus the size of s.
Work out exactly when two foam triangles overlap. With s at most d, which pairs of trees can interact at all?

Each piece has area s squared. On one trunk, pieces with bases y at most y′ overlap iff y′ minus y less than s; on neighbouring trunks (A to B or B to C) they overlap iff y′ minus y less than s plus s′ minus d; A and C never overlap. If you add pieces in increasing base height, only the highest piece already placed on each tree can clash with the next one, so the state is a triple: a 3D DP.
clips.script: Each piece has area s squared. On one trunk, pieces with bases y at most y′ overlap iff y′ minus y less than s; on neighbouring trunks (eh to B or B to C) they overlap iff y′ minus y less than s plus s′ minus d; eh and C never overlap. If you add pieces in increasing base height, only the highest piece already placed on each tree can clash with the next one, so the state is a triple: a 3D DP.

clips.text: Sort all positions by base height and let dp of A, b, c be the best area when A, b, c are the last pieces chosen on trees A, B, C. From each state try every later position that clashes with none of A, b, c and add s squared. That is O of N⁴ for N at most 100 positions per tree, which passes if tight; keeping running maxima over lower states brings it to O of N cubed.
clips.script: Sort all positions by base height and let dp of eh, b, c be the best area when eh, b, c are the last pieces chosen on trees eh, B, C. From each state try every later position that clashes with none of eh, b, c and add s squared. That is O of N⁴ for N at most 100 positions per tree, which passes if tight; keeping running maxima over lower states brings it to O of N cubed.

clips.text: Overlap is decided by base heights alone: same trunk needs a gap of at least s, adjacent trunks need y′ minus y at least s plus s′ minus d, and trunks 2d apart never meet. Sorting all positions by base, a set of pieces is valid iff each piece avoids the highest earlier piece on each tree, because lower pieces end below those. So dp over (last on A, last on B, last on C) with transitions to any later non-clashing position is correct; the naive version is O of N⁴, and the jury reduces it to O of N cubed with auxiliary tables. Answers reach about 3 times 10 to the 16, so use 64-bit integers.
clips.script: Overlap is decided by base heights alone: same trunk needs a gap of at least s, adjacent trunks need y′ minus y at least s plus s′ minus d, and trunks 2d apart never meet. Sorting all positions by base, a set of pieces is valid iff each piece avoids the highest earlier piece on each tree, because lower pieces end below those. So dp over (last on eh, last on B, last on C) with transitions to any later non-clashing position is correct; the naive version is O of N⁴, and the jury reduces it to O of N cubed with auxiliary tables. Answers reach about 3 times 10 to the 16, so use 64-bit integers.

clips.text: Arriving somewhere earlier is never worse, since you can always wait. So what does a state need to remember: just how many pints you have had and where you had the last one?

DP over (pints drunk, pub of the last pint) storing the earliest time that pint is finished. Moving between pubs always uses the fastest route, so precompute all-pairs travel times with Floyd–Warshall (k at most 300).

best of 1, y is dist(1, y) plus t 1 if that is at most c y. best of p plus 1, y is min over pubs x is not y of best of p, x plus dist(x, y) plus t_(p plus 1), kept only if at most c y. The answer is the largest p with any finite state; O of k cubed plus r times k squared.

Run Floyd–Warshall on the road network (taking the shortest of parallel roads). Then fill earliest of p, y, the earliest time you can finish pint p at pub y, from earliest of p minus 1, x for x is not y, discarding values after pub y's closing time; the first pint may be at any pub, reached from pub 1. The answer is the largest p with a reachable state. O of k cubed plus r times k squared about 3.6 times 10 to the 7 operations.
Removing stop i merges the two drives next to it into one. Which drives stay exactly as they were?

Every other drive is unchanged, so the new longest drive is max(merged drive, longest other drive). Prefix and suffix maxima of the gaps give the longest other drive in O of 1; even simpler, the original longest drive never goes away, it either survives or is swallowed by a longer merged drive.
Let G be the longest original gap and M the minimum over interior stops of s_(i plus 1) minus s_(i minus 1). The answer is max(G, M), found in one pass.

Removing interior stop i gives a longest drive of max(s_(i plus 1) minus s_(i minus 1), G), because the original maximum G either stays or is contained in the merged drive. So the answer is max(G, min over i of s_(i plus 1) minus s_(i minus 1)). One O of n pass; the version with prefix and suffix maxima of the gaps is equally fast.
The order of the letters does not matter at all, only how many times each letter appears.
Each letter must appear at least as often as in A and at least as often as in b, and nothing more is required. So the shortest amalgram has max(count in A, count in b) copies of each letter.
clips.script: Each letter must appear at least as often as in eh and at least as often as in b, and nothing more is required. So the shortest amalgram has max(count in eh, count in b) copies of each letter.

clips.text: Count the 26 letters in both words and print each letter max(ca of c, cb of c) times. O of the size of A plus the size of b; read the 10 to the 6-character lines with fast input.
clips.script: Count the 26 letters in both words and print each letter max(ca of c, cb of c) times. O of the size of eh plus the size of b; read the 10 to the 6-character lines with fast input.

clips.text: The shortest amalgram uses exactly max(cnt a(c), cnt b(c)) copies of each letter c, which is both necessary and sufficient. Count, then print the letters in any order. The jury alternative sorts both words and merges them with two pointers, printing a common letter once. O of the size of A plus the size of b.
clips.script: The shortest amalgram uses exactly max(cnt a(c), cnt b(c)) copies of each letter c, which is both necessary and sufficient. Count, then print the letters in any order. The jury alternative sorts both words and merges them with two pointers, printing a common letter once. O of the size of eh plus the size of b.

clips.text: Each query fits its own model, and both the months and the queries number up to 10 to the 6. Which quantities about the months L to R does the best K and B actually depend on?

Set both partial derivatives of p(K, B) to zero: you get a 2 times 2 linear system whose coefficients only use the count, sum of x, sum of y, sum of x squared and sum of xy over the range. Four prefix-sum arrays give those in O of 1 per query.

Solve (Sxx plus λ) times K plus Sx times B is Sxy and Sx times K plus (cnt plus λ) times B is Sy by Cramer's rule and print K times X plus B. Keep the prefix sums in long double (they reach 10 to the 8 and you subtract them), and use fast I/O for two million lines.

The penalty is a convex quadratic in (K, B), so the minimum is where both partial derivatives vanish, a 2 times 2 system in cnt, sum of x, sum of y, sum of x squared and sum of xy over months L to R. Precompute prefix sums of x, y, x squared and xy; each query takes O of 1: det is (Sxx plus λ)(cnt plus λ) minus Sx squared, K is (Sxy times (cnt plus λ) minus Sx times Sy) / det, B is ((Sxx plus λ) times Sy minus Sx times Sxy) / det. Total O of n plus m. Precision is the main risk, so use long double for the sums.
Between two checkpoints the shortest route runs straight. At a checkpoint, what can it do: pass straight through, bounce off it, or turn around one of its endpoints?

A bounce off a checkpoint is a mirror reflection, and it disappears if you reflect the rest of the course across that checkpoint's line (unfolding). With n at most 16 you can afford to try every subset of bouncing checkpoints; what remains is a shortest path whose only real turns are at checkpoint endpoints.

For each mirror pattern, build the reflected checkpoints. Nodes are the start, the end and the checkpoint endpoints; a node on checkpoint i connects to a node on checkpoint j greater than i iff the straight segment between them meets the (reflected) checkpoints i plus 1 … j minus 1 in order. Edges only go forward in checkpoint order, so a DP over the nodes gives the shortest route; take the best over all patterns.

A shortest route bends only at checkpoints, either reflecting off one at equal angles or turning around an endpoint. The jury removes reflections by enumerating the 2 to the n choices of reflecting checkpoints and mirroring the later course, then solves a shortest path over start, end and endpoints, where an edge exists iff its segment crosses every intermediate (mirrored) checkpoint in the required order. Since edges go forward in checkpoint order the shortest path is a DP, and the 15 s limit covers the enumeration; enumerating the reflection choices only for the checkpoints between each pair of endpoints is cheaper still. Treat touching a checkpoint (including at an endpoint or along a collinear stretch) as crossing it.
Three equations and four unknowns leave one free variable. Write every flap in terms of it.

With n is A, the equations give e is σ minus A, s is A minus r and w is σ minus p minus A, where σ is (p plus r plus y) over 2. So you minimise max(the size of A minus 0, the size of A minus σ, the size of A minus r, the size of A minus (σ minus p)): the largest distance from A to four points on a line.
clips.script: With n is eh, the equations give e is σ minus eh, s is eh minus r and w is σ minus p minus eh, where σ is (p plus r plus y) over 2. So you minimise max(the size of eh minus 0, the size of eh minus σ, the size of eh minus r, the size of eh minus (σ minus p)): the largest distance from eh to four points on a line.

clips.text: The best A is the midpoint of the smallest and largest of 0, σ, r, σ minus p; then compute e, s and w from it. O of 1 per request. The jury alternatives are to binary-search the maximum T, or to try each pair of flaps with equal absolute value.
clips.script: The best eh is the midpoint of the smallest and largest of 0, σ, r, σ minus p; then compute e, s and w from it. O of 1 per request. The jury alternatives are to binary-search the maximum T, or to try each pair of flaps with equal absolute value.

clips.text: Eliminate variables: e plus n is (p plus r plus y) over 2, which is σ, s is n minus r, w is e minus p, so with n is a all four flaps are A minus a constant from 0, σ, r, σ minus p (up to sign). Minimising the maximum distance from A to a set of points on a line puts A at the midpoint of the extreme points, giving the optimum (max minus min) over 2. Output n is A, e is σ minus A, s is A minus r, w is σ minus p minus A; this reproduces every sample line. The jury's binary search on T is a valid alternative.
clips.script: Eliminate variables: e plus n is (p plus r plus y) over 2, which is σ, s is n minus r, w is e minus p, so with n is a all four flaps are eh minus a constant from 0, σ, r, σ minus p (up to sign). Minimising the maximum distance from eh to a set of points on a line puts eh at the midpoint of the extreme points, giving the optimum (max minus min) over 2. Output n is eh, e is σ minus eh, s is eh minus r, w is σ minus p minus eh; this reproduces every sample line. The jury's binary search on T is a valid alternative.

clips.text: The climbers you keep must be non-decreasing in height. What decides the cost is, for each kept climber, which kept climber came just before.

It is the longest-non-decreasing-subsequence DP with a different score: dp of x is min over earlier kept i with h i at most h x of dp of i plus (x minus i minus 1) squared. Add a height minus infinity climber before the start and +infinity after the end so the end gaps count. O of n squared is too slow for 10 to the 6, and the square makes each candidate a line in x: convex hull trick.

With X is x minus 1, dp of i plus (X minus i) squared is X squared plus (dp of i plus i squared) minus 2i times X, a line with slope minus 2i. Keep a Fenwick tree over compressed heights whose nodes hold lower hulls of these lines: insert line i into the nodes covering heights at least h i and query the prefix of heights at most h x. Slopes arrive in decreasing order and queries in increasing X, so each hull is a deque with a moving pointer: O of n log n.

With sentinels at both ends, dp of x is min(dp of i plus (x minus i minus 1) squared) over i less than x with h i at most h x, and the answer is dp at the right sentinel. Rewriting the cost as a line in x lets a convex hull answer the minimum, and the height condition is handled like LIS with a Fenwick tree whose nodes are hulls (the jury slides call them lists of lines sorted by gradient). Insertions are in slope order and queries in x order, so each node is a monotone deque and the total is O of n log n. Costs reach 10 to the 12, so use 64-bit values and 128-bit (or long double) for the hull comparisons.
Recomputing each candidate's distance to every chosen protein costs O of k times l per candidate per step, around 6 times 10 to the 10 operations in total. What changes between one step and the next?

Only one protein joins the chosen set per step, so each candidate's minimum distance to the set can be updated with a single new distance. Keep best of v is min distance from v to the chosen proteins (farthest-point sampling).

Choose p(1) as the farthest from protein 1 and set best of v is D(v, p(1)). Then repeatedly pick the first v not yet chosen (scanning in input order with strict >) with the largest best of v, print it, and update best of v is min(best of v, D(v, new)) for all v. O of k times n times l about 2.6 times 10 to the 8 cheap operations.

The rule picks the protein maximising its minimum distance to the chosen set, and that minimum only ever shrinks by one new distance per step. Maintain it in an array: after each choice, one pass over all n proteins computes D(v, new) in O of l and updates the minimum. Only proteins not yet chosen are candidates (with duplicate embeddings, a chosen one could otherwise tie at distance 0). Ties go to the earliest protein, so scan in input order with a strict comparison. Total O of k times n times l, well within 5 s.

Comparing the key at every position costs rk times ck per position, about 10 to the 12 steps at worst. You need each position checked in O of 1, and then a fast way to mark every cell that lies inside some match.

A 2D rolling (polynomial) hash checks each position in O of 1: hash every length-ck window of each row, then roll a second hash down each column over rk of those row hashes. Marking cells covered by at least one match is adding 1 on rectangles: a 2D difference array.

Compute the key's hash the same way and compare it with the block hash at every top-left corner (use mod 2 to the 61 minus 1 or two moduli). For each match add +1 and minus 1 at the four corners of its rectangle, take 2D prefix sums, and print the haystack character where the count is positive, "." elsewhere. O of rh times ch.

Hash rows with one base, then columns of row hashes with another, to get the hash of every rk times ck block in O of rh times ch; positions whose hash is the key's are matches. Each match covers a rectangle, so record it with four updates in a 2D difference array and recover coverage with prefix sums. Print the original character where coverage is positive. The jury also mentions Aho–Corasick on rows followed by matching the column pattern of row-match ids.

Grow the new shape from a tiny copy around the origin. Whether k times A fits inside B can only change at scales where the boundaries touch, a vertex of one polygon lying on an edge of the other; and because the shapes are not convex, the scales that fit need not form a single interval.

Look along rays from the origin. Scaling moves a vertex v of A along its own ray to k times the size of v, so where that ray crosses B tells you the ranges of k for which v is inside B; symmetrically, the ray through a vertex u of B tells you when u is not inside k times A. Every vertex yields a set of allowed k-ranges.
clips.script: Look along rays from the origin. Scaling moves a vertex v of A along its own ray to k times the size of v, so where that ray crosses B tells you the ranges of k for which v is inside B; symmetrically, the ray through a vertex u of B tells you when u is not inside k times eh. Every vertex yields a set of allowed k-ranges.

clips.text: Compute the allowed ranges for every vertex of both polygons (O of (n plus m) squared ray–edge intersections) and sweep over k to find the largest scale allowed by all of them. Rays often pass exactly through other vertices, so do the intersections in exact rational arithmetic and handle tangent and collinear cases deliberately.

The jury reduces the problem to one dimension along rays from the origin: containment can only break when a vertex of k times A meets an edge of B or a vertex of B meets an edge of k times A. For each vertex they slice both shapes along its ray, turn the slices into the ranges of k in which that vertex is on the correct side, and intersect all ranges with a sweep line over k, printing the largest feasible scale. Coordinates are integers up to 10 to the 4, so the critical scales are ratios of small integers and rational arithmetic keeps the many tangent cases exact. Expect most of the effort to go into robustness.
clips.script: The jury reduces the problem to one dimension along rays from the origin: containment can only break when a vertex of k times A meets an edge of B or a vertex of B meets an edge of k times eh. For each vertex they slice both shapes along its ray, turn the slices into the ranges of k in which that vertex is on the correct side, and intersect all ranges with a sweep line over k, printing the largest feasible scale. Coordinates are integers up to 10 to the 4, so the critical scales are ratios of small integers and rational arithmetic keeps the many tangent cases exact. Expect most of the effort to go into robustness.

clips.text: In the example, team Y attempts most of its problems in the category where everybody does well. Team X can win every category narrowly while spending its attempts where both teams do badly.

Think of each category as two vectors (b, A) and (d, c): X needs the steeper vector in every category, but the sums must swap order. Put almost all of Y's attempts into one category where X is perfect (1 over 1) and Y is nearly perfect, and put most of X's attempts where both score around a third.
clips.script: Think of each category as two vectors (b, eh) and (d, c): X needs the steeper vector in every category, but the sums must swap order. Put almost all of Y's attempts into one category where X is perfect (1 over 1) and Y is nearly perfect, and put most of X's attempts where both score around a third.

clips.text: One construction for M at least 4N: category 1: X is 1 over 1, Y is (D minus 1)/D with D, which is M minus 3(N minus 1); categories 2 … N minus 1: X is 1 over 2, Y is 1 over 3; category N: Y is 1 over 3 and X is x/B with B, which is M minus 1 minus 2(N minus 2), x is floor of B over 3 plus 1. Both teams attempt M, X wins every category, and X solves N minus 1 plus x less than M minus 2N plus 1 is Y's total.

This is the jury construction: one category where X scores 1 over 1 and Y scores (D minus 1)/D on almost all of its attempts, N minus 2 categories of 1 over 2 against 1 over 3, and a last category where X scores just over a third of its remaining B attempts against Y's 1 over 3. Both attempt totals equal M, every per-category ratio favours X, and Y's solved total M minus 2N plus 1 exceeds X's N minus 1 plus floor of B over 3 plus 1 whenever M greater than 3.5N, which M at least 4N guarantees. Output in O of N.
Removing a cable splits the tree into two parts, and the new cable must join them. For a demand between the two parts, how does its new path length depend on the two computers you connect?

A crossing demand (s, t, c) costs c times (dist(s, u) plus 1 plus dist(v, t)), which separates into a cost of u inside one part and a cost of v inside the other. Finding the vertex that minimises a weighted sum of distances in a tree is a rerooting DP.

For each step, weight each vertex by the packets of crossing demands it sends, compute f(root) with one DFS per part and then f(child) is f(parent) plus W minus 2 times W sub(child) for every vertex. On each side pick the smallest-numbered vertex of minimum f among those with fewer than 3 cables, print the pair in increasing order, and apply the change to the tree. O of n times (n plus d) overall.

Demands inside one part keep their distances, so only crossing demands matter and their total is f1(u) plus f2(v) plus (sum of their packets), where fi is a weighted distance sum within part i. Rerooting computes fi for every vertex in O of size after one subtree-weight DFS, so each of the n minus 1 steps costs O of n plus d. Because the optimal pairs are all combinations of the minimisers on each side, the tie-break is met by taking the smallest-numbered minimiser on each side (skipping vertices that already have 3 cables). Keep the modified tree for the next step; values reach about 10 to the 16, so use 64-bit integers.
Fill the stripes left to right. At each new stripe, which colours are allowed, and among those, which one would you least regret using?

Greedy: the allowed colours are those not among the previous p minus 1 stripes, and taking the least-used allowed colour keeps the most frequent colour growing as slowly as possible. A priority queue keyed by usage count serves this in O of log k per stripe.

First check that the given stripes never repeat a colour within p consecutive stripes. Put every colour not in the last p minus 1 stripes into a min-heap of (count, colour); for each new stripe pop the least-used colour, append it, and push back the colour of the stripe that just left the window with its current count. If the heap is ever empty, print impossible.

Validate the prefix, then extend greedily: at each position use the allowed colour with the smallest count so far. A min-heap holds exactly the colours outside the last p minus 1 stripes; after placing stripe i, the colour of stripe i minus p plus 1 becomes usable again and goes back in. If the heap is empty when a stripe is still needed (fewer than p colours and a long enough scarf), no valid scarf exists. O of (n plus k) log k; as the jury notes, check the finished scarf is valid.
Classify each exercise first, and mind the order of the checks: "restarms" is a rest day and "delegation" is a leg day.

Pure implementation: a name containing "rest" is rest, otherwise one containing "leg" is legs, otherwise arms. Pick one fixed character per type from the Supplementary Multilingual Plane whose Unicode name contains the required word.

For example U plus 1F9B5 LEG, U plus 1F4AA FLEXED BICEPS and U plus 1F634 SLEEPING FACE. Day d (0-based) uses exercise d mod n; print weeks 1 to 4 with seven days and week 5 with three, each line starting with the week number and a space, writing the UTF-8 bytes directly.

Map each exercise to rest, leg or arm by substring checks in that order, then print 31 days as 4 full weeks plus 3 days, cycling through the plan. Use one fixed emoji per type whose Unicode name contains face, leg, or arm/biceps. In C plus plus just print the UTF-8 bytes; in Java set the output encoding to UTF-8.
The professor's loop is cubic only if there are about N rounds and each round makes about N squared comparisons. When does an essay compare against many others without being postponed?

Construction: essays that do not dominate each other (an antichain in deviation versus quality) never postpone each other, so each one scans all later ones. Add essays that dominate the antichain, arranged so that only one essay gets marked per round.

Put K is floor of N over 2 antichain essays first (deviation i and quality i for i is 1 … K), then N minus K essays with word count exactly W and qualities 501, 502, …. These form a chain that dominates the whole antichain, so each round marks only the best remaining chain essay, while every antichain essay scans the rest of the antichain before meeting the chain: about N cubed/16 at least N cubed/20 comparisons.

Make the first half pairwise incomparable and the second half a chain that dominates all of them. In every round each antichain essay compares with all later antichain essays and is then postponed by the first chain essay, each chain essay but the last is postponed by its successor, and only the best chain essay is marked, so for N over 2 rounds each round costs about K squared over 2 comparisons, N cubed/16 in total (about 6.3 times 10 to the 7 for N is 1000, above the 5 times 10 to the 7 needed). Use word counts W plus i, or W minus i when W plus K greater than 10 to the 4, so all values stay in range and all pairs are distinct. The jury's slides use the mirror image: their remaining N minus K essays are dominated by the last N minus K antichain essays instead of dominating the antichain, so each round marks two essays, one from each group. Either way there are O of N rounds of O of N squared comparisons.
Each card alternates between tapping in and tapping out. What do you need to remember per card?
Pure bookkeeping: store, for every card, the pier where its open trip started (or none), and settle the trip when the card taps again.

On a tap: if the card has no open trip, record the pier; otherwise charge the size of i minus j, or 100 if it is the same pier, and close the trip. After all events charge 100 for every trip still open. O of m plus k.

Keep start of card is minus 1 when no trip is open. Scan the events: an idle card opens a trip at the pier, an active card closes it and pays the size of i minus j, or £100 if it tapped out where it tapped in. Finally every card with an open trip pays £100. The jury alternative fines £100 at tap-in and refunds it on a valid tap-out.
All posts lie on one circle and the fence connects them in angular order. How can you write the enclosed area as a sum over consecutive chosen posts?

Splitting the polygon into triangles from the centre gives area is sum of ½R squared times sin(θ_next minus θ_cur) over consecutive chosen posts (signed, so it still works when the centre is outside). The area is a sum of terms that each depend on two consecutive choices: a DP over chosen posts in order.

Fix the first chosen post S. Let dp of j, c be the best area of a chain from S to post j using c posts; dp of j, c is max over i less than j of dp of i, c minus 1 plus ½R squared times sin(θ_j minus θ_i), and close the polygon with the triangle from the last post back to S. Try every S: O of n cubed times p about 10 to the 8 simple steps.

Represent the polygon by its chosen posts in increasing angle; its area is the sum of signed centre triangles ½R squared times sin(Δθ) for consecutive posts, including the wrap-around pair. For every starting post S, a DP over (last post, posts used) maximises the chain area, and the closing triangle back to S completes it. Using more posts never hurts, but taking the maximum over all counts up to p is just as easy. Remember R is 1000 m and convert degrees to radians.
The strongest courier can never be a median. Which teammates should the second-strongest courier have so that their strength counts?
Greedy: pair the two strongest couriers in one team (the second one becomes the median) and give them the weakest courier, who is useless anywhere else. Repeat on the rest.
Sort strengths in decreasing order and sum the elements at positions 2, 4, …, 2 times (n over 3) (1-based). Use 64-bit integers; O of n log n.

Sort descending. The best team takes couriers 1 and 2 plus the weakest remaining courier, scoring courier 2; repeating gives the sum of every second element of the sorted list, n over 3 of them. An exchange argument shows no grouping does better. The sum can reach 3.3 times 10 to the 11, so use 64-bit integers.
There are 2 to the 30 about 10 to the 9 possible spells, and scoring each from scratch costs O of n squared. Can you split the symbols into two halves?

Meet in the middle: split the symbols into halves of 15. A spell's strength is (pairs inside the left half) plus (pairs inside the right half) plus (cross pairs). The cross term couples the halves, so you cannot just combine the best of each side, but it can be built up one symbol at a time.

Precompute the inner strength g of R of every right mask. For each left mask L, compute w j is sum of over i in L of d_(i,j) for each right symbol j, then sweep all right masks with cross of R is cross of R without its lowest bit plus w_(lowest bit) and keep the best f of L plus g of R plus cross of R. That is 2 to the 15 times 2 to the 15 about 10 to the 9 O of 1 steps, fine in 4.2 s with tight loops.

Split the n at most 30 symbols into two halves and precompute the inner strengths of all subsets of each half incrementally. For each left subset, the cross contribution of a right subset is a sum of per-symbol weights, so all 2 to the 15 right subsets can be scored in O of 1 each by extending from the subset without its lowest bit. This brute-forces all 2 to the 30 combinations at O of 1 apiece, as the jury suggests. The empty spell is allowed (print 0 and an empty line), and symbols can be printed in any order.
Right after an advert the timer resets, so where the next advert falls depends only on which song you are at. Adverts jump you from song to song.

Let next(i) be the song after which the advert falls when you start fresh at song i: the first point where the running total of durations reaches c, found with two pointers (or prefix sums) on the doubled playlist. Counting adverts is then "how many jumps fit before the end", which binary lifting answers in O of log n.

On positions 0 … 2n minus 1 set nxt of s is j plus 1 for the first j with d s plus … plus d j at least c (or 2n if none) and build jump tables up of b, s. For start i, count the jumps that land at most at i plus n minus 1 (an advert after the last song does not count), trying b from high to low. O of n log n; int32 tables fit in 512 MB.

Adverts are forced as soon as c seconds have passed at a song boundary, so the advert sequence from a start is a chain of next() jumps. Compute next() for every position of the doubled playlist with two pointers, build binary-lifting tables, and for each start i count the jumps that stay within the n songs, excluding an advert after the final song. That is O of n log n for n is 10 to the 6. If c exceeds the total duration, next() never fires and every answer is 0.
At time t the follower is at arc length t along the track and the leader at t plus s. When does the formula for the distance between them change?

Only when one of them passes a vertex. Between those moments both walk in straight lines at unit speed, so their difference vector is linear in t and the squared distance is a convex quadratic, which you can minimise exactly (or by ternary search).

Merge the breakpoints L k (follower at vertex k) and L k minus s (leader at vertex k) with two pointers over t in 0 to L minus s. On each piece take the difference D0 at its start and w is u leader minus u follower, minimise the size of D0 plus w times τ squared over the piece by clamping τ is minus (D0 times w)/the size of w squared, and keep the minimum. O of n.

Parametrise by the follower's arc length t; the leader is at t plus s. Cut 0 to L minus s at every time either walker reaches a vertex; on each piece both move linearly, so the distance is minimised in closed form (the jury also allows ternary search on each piece). Two pointers walk both positions along the polyline in O of n. The track can be about 3 times 10 to the 12 m long, so keep cumulative lengths in long double and compute positions relative to segment starts.

Range additions plus range questions, 3 times 10 to the 5 of each: you need a segment tree. What small summary of a range lets you answer "are the local minima increasing?" and lets you combine two neighbouring ranges?

Use a lazy segment tree. Adding d to a whole node shifts every stored value but never changes the up/down pattern or the validity inside it, so it is a lazy tag; merging two halves can only create or remove a local minimum at the seam.

Per node keep: first and last value, direction of the first and last non-flat step, the first and last local minimum strictly inside, and whether the inside minima increase. On merge, a valley appears at the seam if the last non-flat step on the left is down and the next non-flat step is up (equal values across the seam are flat); check the order across the seam. For a query, also count the first element as a minimum if the first step is up and the last if the last step is down.

Store in every segment-tree node a summary of its range: endpoints, the first and last non-flat step directions, the first and last interior valley values, and a validity flag. Merging checks for a valley at the seam (collapsing equal values) and that valleys stay strictly increasing across it; a range add only shifts the stored values, so it is a lazy tag, as in the jury solution. A query merges O of log n nodes and then adds the end elements as minima when the sequence starts by rising or ends by falling. O of (n plus m) log n.

Fix which pin goes into which hole first: earth to earth, and the other two either way, so only two assignments. Then a pin of radius r fits a hole of radius R exactly when its centre is within R minus r of the hole's centre.

So shrink each pin to a point and each hole to a disk of radius R minus r: the question becomes whether a rigid triangle (rotations and translations, no reflection) can have each vertex in its own disk. If it can, it can with two of the vertices on the boundary of their disks.

Try each pair of vertices as the pair on the boundary: put the first on its circle at angle φ, put the second on its circle at the right distance (a circle–circle intersection), which fixes the rotation and so the third vertex; minimise the third vertex's excess distance over φ with fine sampling plus ternary search. Handle disks of radius 0 and output the transformed pin centres.

Enumerate the two pin-to-hole assignments, shrink pins to points and holes to disks of radius R minus r (negative means impossible). A rigid placement with each vertex in its disk exists iff one exists with two vertices on their circles, so parametrise one boundary vertex by an angle, place the second by circle–circle intersection, and check the third; the jury describes this as case analysis plus ternary search. The tolerances in the statement (10 to the -6 fit, 2 times 10 to the -6 guarantee for NO) allow a numeric search. Nobody solved it in the contest.
Every flight goes strictly forward in time, so the states (airport, time) form a DAG. What single number per flight would let you answer every cancellation quickly?

Build the time-expanded graph implicitly: let V(f) be the earliest arrival at the final destination if you board flight f, computed by DP over flights in decreasing departure time. Cancelling f removes only f itself from the choices at its airport and minute.

V(f) is arr(f) if f lands at the destination, else the minimum V(g) over flights g leaving f's arrival airport at or after arr(f) (per-airport lists sorted by departure with suffix minima). For a cancelled itinerary flight f, take the minimum V(g) over g is not f leaving the same airport at or after dep(f) (keep the two best per minute to exclude f), or dep(f) itself if that airport is the destination. The answer is the largest delay against the planned arrival, 0 if none, stranded if any is infinite.

The jury builds a graph with a vertex per (airport, interesting time), flight edges and waiting edges, and propagates earliest arrival at the destination backwards; because time only increases, this is a DP over flights by decreasing departure time. For each itinerary flight, the recovery time is the best V over the other flights leaving that airport no earlier, which needs the best two values per departure minute so the cancelled flight can be excluded (identical duplicate flights are allowed). If the cancelled flight leaves from the destination airport you are already there. O of n log n with hashing of airport codes and sorting.
You do not need the best acyclic subset, only one with at least half the dependencies. Is there an order of the tasks that makes half of the edges automatically safe?

A set of edges that all go forward in one fixed order is acyclic, which is exactly what a topological order means. In the order 1 … n every dependency goes either up (A less than b) or down (A greater than b).
clips.script: A set of edges that all go forward in one fixed order is acyclic, which is exactly what a topological order means. In the order 1 … n every dependency goes either up (eh less than b) or down (eh greater than b).

clips.text: Split the dependencies into those with A less than b and those with A greater than b. Each class is acyclic (task numbers strictly increase, or strictly decrease, along any path), and the larger one has at least m over 2 edges, so the answer is always YES with the larger class. O of n plus m.
clips.script: Split the dependencies into those with eh less than b and those with eh greater than b. Each class is acyclic (task numbers strictly increase, or strictly decrease, along any path), and the larger one has at least m over 2 edges, so the answer is always YES with the larger class. O of n plus m.

clips.text: Classify each dependency as increasing (A less than b) or decreasing (A greater than b); since A is not b, every edge is one or the other. Neither class can contain a cycle, because the task number changes monotonically along its edges. Print YES and the ids of the larger class, which has at least half the edges.
clips.script: Classify each dependency as increasing (eh less than b) or decreasing (eh greater than b); since eh is not b, every edge is one or the other. Neither class can contain a cycle, because the task number changes monotonically along its edges. Print YES and the ids of the larger class, which has at least half the edges.

clips.text: Firing as early as possible is always best. How many missiles does each unit need, and when does the last of them leave?

Unit 1 needs k1 is ceiling of h2 / d1 hits and fires them at times 0, t1, 2t1, …, so its killing missile leaves at (k1 minus 1) times t1 and lands half a second later. Compare that with unit 2's (k2 minus 1) times t2, where k2 is ceiling of h1 / d2.

If (k1 minus 1) times t1 less than (k2 minus 1) times t2 player one wins, if greater player two wins, and if equal both killing missiles are already in the air: draw. Times are integers, so the 0.5 s flight never changes the order.

Each unit fires every t seconds from time 0 and needs ceiling of h opponent over d hits, so it fires its fatal missile at (hits minus 1) times t. The unit whose fatal missile leaves strictly earlier wins, because its opponent dies 0.5 s later, before its own next launch at an integer time. Equal launch times mean both are destroyed: draw.
Count cells: a 2 times n rectangle has 2n cells, squares and S-tiles have 4 and corners have 3. What does that say about how many corners you can use?

Squares always fit and add 2 each. S-tiles cannot close a rectangle on their own, but a row of S-tiles can be capped by one corner at each end, and the remaining corners pair up into 2 times 3 blocks.

Answer is 2a, plus, if c at least 2, 2b plus 3 times floor of c over 2 (two corners cap all the S-tiles, the other corners pair up). With c less than 2 the S-tiles are useless and corners alone cannot be used.

An even number of corners must be used (cell parity), and S-tiles need corners at both ends of their chain. With at least two corners, all b S-tiles fit between two corners, forming a block of width 3 plus 2b, and the other corners pair into width-3 blocks. So the width is 2a plus (c at least 2? 2b plus 3 times floor of c over 2: 0).
Names only need to be consistent for equal sizes and different for different sizes. "1L" and "1.0L" are the same size written differently.
Bring every volume to a canonical text form, then map that text to letters with a fixed one-to-one rule, so equal sizes get equal names and different sizes get different names.

Drop the trailing L; if there is a decimal point, strip trailing zeros and then a bare trailing point (never strip zeros from "1000"). Map digits 0 to 9 to A to j and the point to z, and print the result.
clips.script: Drop the trailing L; if there is a decimal point, strip trailing zeros and then a bare trailing point (never strip zeros from "1000"). Map digits 0 to 9 to eh to j and the point to z, and print the result.

clips.text: Canonicalise each volume string by removing the unit, then trailing zeros after a decimal point, then a dangling point. Translate the canonical string character by character into lowercase letters with an injective map. Parsing to double and using a map also works narrowly, but the string method avoids precision issues with ten decimal digits.
